name: Homer
birthplace: Ionia (traditionally; birthplace claimed by several cities)
bio: The name the ancient Greeks gave to the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, the founding epics of Western literature. Whether a single Homer ever existed is one of the oldest questions in literary scholarship.
bio_full: Nothing reliable is known about Homer's life. Ancient tradition pictured him as a blind singer from the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, and seven cities, among them Smyrna and Chios, claimed to be his birthplace. Modern scholars generally date the two epics to the late eighth or seventh century BC. Since the work of Milman Parry in the 1930s, it has been widely accepted that they grew out of a long tradition of oral composition, in which singers improvised in hexameter using stock phrases and scenes. Whether one poet, two poets or a whole tradition stands behind the poems, and when exactly they were fixed in writing, remains debated; the so-called Homeric Question has never been settled.

Whoever composed them, the Iliad and the Odyssey were the shared foundation of Greek culture: children learned to read from them, philosophers argued with them, and tragedians took their plots from the stories around them. Their formulaic epithets, extended similes and vivid scenes of war, homecoming and grief became the model for epic from Virgil to Milton. Through translation, from Chapman and Pope to modern versions, Homer has never ceased to be read, and the Odyssey in particular supplied the template for countless journeys in later literature, including Joyce's Ulysses.

name: Sappho
bio: The great lyric poet of archaic Greece, admired in antiquity as the tenth Muse. Her intense, personal poems of love and longing survive mainly in fragments.
bio_full: Sappho lived on the island of Lesbos around 600 BC, probably in the city of Mytilene, into an aristocratic family. Ancient sources mention brothers, a daughter named Kleis and a period of exile in Sicily, but most stories about her life, including the legend that she leapt from a cliff for love of a ferryman, are later inventions. She composed songs to be sung to the lyre, many apparently for performance among circles of young women. Alexandrian scholars collected her poems into nine books, but only one complete poem, the Ode to Aphrodite, and a few substantial fragments survived the Middle Ages; papyrus finds, including two new poems published in 2014, have added more.

Sappho wrote in her local Aeolic dialect, in metres that include the stanza later named after her. Her poems speak in the first person about desire, jealousy, memory and the beauty of the beloved, with a precision and immediacy that later readers found startlingly modern. Plato is said to have called her the tenth Muse, and Catullus translated her. Because her love poetry is often addressed to women, her name and her island gave English the words sapphic and lesbian. The very fragmentary state of her work has itself inspired poets and translators, from Swinburne to Anne Carson.

name: Aeschylus
bio: The earliest of the three great Athenian tragedians, often called the father of tragedy. His Oresteia trilogy traces the passage from blood vengeance to civic justice.
bio_full: Aeschylus was born around 525 BC at Eleusis near Athens into a noble family. He fought against the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC, where his brother was killed, and probably also at Salamis, and his epitaph is said to have recorded his war service rather than his plays. He began competing at the Athenian festival of the Great Dionysia in the 490s and won first prize there thirteen times. He wrote perhaps seventy to ninety plays, of which seven survive under his name, including The Persians, Seven Against Thebes, The Suppliants and the Oresteia of 458 BC. He made visits to Sicily at the invitation of the tyrant Hieron and died at Gela around 456 BC.

Aristotle credits Aeschylus with adding a second actor to the single actor and chorus of early tragedy, which made real dramatic conflict possible. His language is grand, dense and rich in metaphor, and his choruses carry much of the weight of the drama. He typically worked in connected trilogies, following a curse or a moral problem across generations, and his plays wrestle with the justice of Zeus and the suffering through which, as the Oresteia says, humans learn. The authorship of Prometheus Bound, traditionally his, is now debated. His work set the scale and seriousness of tragedy for everything that followed.

name: Sophocles
bio: The Athenian tragedian whose Oedipus the King Aristotle held up as the model of tragedy. Seven of his more than 120 plays survive.
bio_full: Sophocles was born around 497 BC at Colonus, just outside Athens, the son of a wealthy man. He was famous for his good looks and musical talent, and as a youth is said to have led the chorus celebrating the victory at Salamis. He won his first victory at the Dionysia in 468 BC, defeating Aeschylus, and went on to win more often than any other tragedian, never placing lower than second. He also served Athens in public life, as a treasurer and as one of the generals alongside Pericles in the Samian War. He lived through almost the whole of the city's classical greatness and died in 406 BC, shortly before its defeat by Sparta.

Sophocles is credited with introducing a third actor and with painted scenery, and he gave up the connected trilogy in favour of self-contained plays. His surviving works, including Ajax, Antigone, Oedipus the King, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus, are admired for their tight construction, their dramatic irony and their heroes, strong-willed figures who refuse to bend. Aristotle's Poetics drew heavily on Oedipus the King, and through it Sophocles became the standard for tragic form. Antigone and Oedipus have since been reworked endlessly, by Hegel and Freud as much as by dramatists.

name: Euripides
bio: The youngest and most unsettling of the great tragedians, known for his clever women, questioning of the gods and psychological realism. More of his plays survive than of Aeschylus and Sophocles combined.
bio_full: Euripides was born around 480 BC; a later legend placed his birth on the island of Salamis on the day of the great sea battle. He first competed at the Dionysia in 455 BC but won first prize only four times in his life, a sign that his challenging plays divided Athenian audiences. Ancient biographies describe him as a bookish recluse who wrote in a cave, and he was a favourite target of the comic poet Aristophanes. Towards the end of his life he left Athens for the court of King Archelaus of Macedon, where he died around 406 BC. Eighteen or nineteen of his tragedies survive, including Medea, Hippolytus, The Trojan Women, Electra and The Bacchae, which was performed after his death.

Euripides brought the heroes of myth down to human scale and gave unprecedented voice to women, slaves and outsiders. His plays include passionate monologues, sharp debates and sudden endings in which a god appears from the machine. He questioned traditional religion and showed the horrors of war at a time when Athens was fighting Sparta. Aristotle called him the most tragic of the poets. His popularity grew after his death, and his work has been especially influential in the modern theatre, where Medea, The Trojan Women and The Bacchae are among the most staged of all Greek plays.

name: Aristophanes
bio: The great comic playwright of ancient Athens, whose eleven surviving comedies mix political satire, fantasy, obscenity and lyric beauty.
bio_full: Aristophanes was born in Athens around 446 BC and had his first play staged in 427 BC, while still very young. He wrote about forty comedies over a career of some forty years, of which eleven survive, among them The Clouds, The Wasps, The Birds, Lysistrata and The Frogs. His work spans the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta and its aftermath. He clashed with the powerful politician Cleon, whom he mocked repeatedly, and in The Clouds he lampooned Socrates as a fraudulent teacher, a portrait Plato later suggested contributed to prejudice against the philosopher. Plato nevertheless gave him a memorable speech about love in the Symposium.

His plays belong to what is called Old Comedy: fantastical plots in which an ordinary citizen makes a private peace with the enemy, founds a city in the clouds or travels to the underworld, combined with personal attacks on living Athenians, choral songs of real lyrical beauty and frank sexual humour. In the parabasis the chorus stepped out to address the audience directly on the poet's behalf. Aristophanes is our main source for what Old Comedy was like, and his mixture of satire and fantasy has influenced writers from Rabelais to modern political satirists.

name: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)
bio: Rome's national poet, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics and the Aeneid. For Dante he was the guide through Hell; for Europe he was the model of the poet.
bio_full: Publius Vergilius Maro was born in 70 BC near Mantua in northern Italy and educated in Cremona, Milan and Rome, where he studied rhetoric and Epicurean philosophy. His first collection, the Eclogues, pastoral poems written in the turmoil after Caesar's assassination, brought him to the attention of Maecenas, the cultural patron of the future emperor Augustus. He then spent seven years on the Georgics, a poem on farming, and devoted the last decade of his life to the Aeneid. In 19 BC he fell ill on a journey to Greece and died at Brundisium. He had asked for the unfinished epic to be burned, but Augustus ordered its publication.

Virgil fused Greek forms, Homer for epic, Theocritus for pastoral and Hesiod for didactic poetry, with Roman themes and an exceptional ear for the music of Latin hexameter. His poetry is marked by a deep sympathy for suffering, a sense of the cost of history and an ambiguous relation to the Augustan order it celebrates. The Aeneid became the school text of Europe for nearly two thousand years. Christians read the fourth Eclogue as a prophecy of Christ, medieval legend made Virgil a magician, and Dante chose him as his guide in the Divine Comedy. Few poets have influenced so many others.

name: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus)
bio: The great Roman lyric poet and satirist of the Augustan age, master of the ode and the verse letter. Phrases such as carpe diem come from him.
bio_full: Quintus Horatius Flaccus was born in 65 BC at Venusia in southern Italy, the son of a freed slave who spent his savings educating him in Rome and Athens. In Athens he joined the republican army of Brutus and fought on the losing side at Philippi in 42 BC. Returning to Rome with his property confiscated, he worked as a treasury clerk and began writing poetry. Virgil introduced him to Maecenas, who became his patron and gave him a farm in the Sabine hills that he celebrated for the rest of his life. He became the leading lyric poet of Augustus's Rome, writing the official hymn for the Secular Games of 17 BC, and died in 8 BC, a few weeks after Maecenas.

Horace's works include the Satires, the Epodes, four books of Odes, two books of Epistles and the verse letter known as the Art of Poetry. He adapted Greek lyric metres to Latin with matchless skill and wrote with urbane irony about friendship, wine, love, the brevity of life and the pleasures of a moderate existence. His Art of Poetry was one of the most influential works of literary criticism ever written, setting the rules of decorum for Renaissance and neoclassical writers. Poets from Petrarch and Ben Jonson to Pope and Auden have imitated him, and many of his phrases became proverbial.

name: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso)
bio: The witty, inventive poet of love and transformation whose Metamorphoses became the main source of classical myth for later Europe. He died in exile on the Black Sea.
bio_full: Publius Ovidius Naso was born in 43 BC at Sulmo, east of Rome, into an equestrian family. He was trained for a legal and political career but abandoned it for poetry and quickly became the most fashionable poet of Augustan Rome with his love elegies, the Amores, the Heroides (verse letters from mythical heroines) and the mock-didactic Art of Love. Around AD 8, at the height of his fame and having just completed the Metamorphoses, he was banished by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea. The cause, which he called a poem and a mistake, has never been explained. He spent his last years writing poems of complaint and pleas for recall, and died in exile around AD 17.

Ovid's poetry is playful, ironic and endlessly inventive, delighting in rhetoric, paradox and psychological insight. In the Metamorphoses he linked some 250 myths of transformation into a continuous story running from the creation of the world to his own day. Medieval readers allegorised him, and for the Renaissance his works were the main storehouse of classical mythology: Shakespeare, Titian, Bernini and countless others drew on them. His tales of Pygmalion, Narcissus, Daphne and Orpheus remain the versions most people know.

name: The Beowulf poet
bio: The anonymous Old English poet who composed Beowulf, the longest surviving epic in Old English. Nothing is known about him.
bio_full: The poet of Beowulf is entirely anonymous. The poem survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, copied by two scribes around AD 1000 and now in the British Library, where it was damaged in the Cotton Library fire of 1731. When it was composed is much debated: estimates range from the seventh to the early eleventh century, with many scholars favouring the eighth. Whether it is the work of one poet or the written form of a longer oral tradition is also debated. The poet was evidently a Christian, writing in England about pagan Scandinavian heroes of an earlier age, and knew the traditional techniques of Germanic alliterative verse intimately.

The poet's art lies in the alliterative line, the dense compound words and metaphors called kennings, and a structure that balances youth and age, triumph and loss. The poem looks back at a heroic past with admiration and melancholy, aware that its heroes lacked the Christian faith of its audience. Little noticed until the nineteenth century, Beowulf was transformed in the twentieth by J. R. R. Tolkien's 1936 lecture, which argued for it as a work of art rather than merely a historical document, and it now stands at the head of English literature.

name: Turold
bio: The name in the last line of the Oxford manuscript of The Song of Roland. Whether Turold was the poet, a scribe or a performer is debated.
bio_full: The oldest and finest manuscript of The Song of Roland, copied in England in the twelfth century and now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, ends with a line saying that here ends the geste which Turoldus declines, an ambiguous verb that may mean composes, recites, transcribes or completes. On this basis the poem is traditionally attributed to a Norman named Turold. Attempts to identify him with real people of the period, such as a bishop of Bayeux or a monk of Fécamp, are speculative. Most scholars date the Oxford version to around 1100, but the poem drew on a much older oral tradition about the defeat of Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux in 778.

Whoever Turold was, the Oxford Roland shows a powerful poetic sensibility: terse, repetitive laisses (stanzas) linked by assonance, sharply drawn scenes, and a stark moral world of loyalty, pride and sacrifice. It is the masterpiece of the chanson de geste, the Old French heroic song, and a founding text of French literature. The figure of Roland passed into Italian romance epic through Boiardo and Ariosto and remained a symbol of heroic loyalty for centuries.

name: Chrétien de Troyes
bio: The twelfth-century French poet who created Arthurian romance, introducing Lancelot and the Holy Grail to European literature.
bio_full: Almost nothing is known about Chrétien de Troyes beyond what he says in his works. He was active at the court of Marie de Champagne, daughter of Eleanor of Aquitaine, at Troyes from about 1160, and later dedicated his final romance to Philip, count of Flanders, who died in 1191. He wrote five Arthurian romances in octosyllabic rhyming couplets: Erec and Enide, Cligès, Yvain or the Knight of the Lion, Lancelot or the Knight of the Cart, and the unfinished Perceval or the Story of the Grail. He also translated Ovid, of which a version of the Philomela story probably survives.

Chrétien took the Celtic and Breton legends of King Arthur and turned them into a new kind of narrative poetry about individual knights, their adventures and their inner conflicts between love and duty. He was among the first to write about courtly love in narrative form, and he gave Lancelot his affair with Queen Guinevere and Perceval his encounter with a mysterious grail. His graceful, ironic, psychologically subtle romances were translated and continued across Europe, and they are the ultimate source of much of the Arthurian legend as later told by Malory, Tennyson and modern novelists and filmmakers.

name: Dante Alighieri
bio: The supreme poet of the Italian language, whose Divine Comedy, a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, is one of the summits of world literature.
bio_full: Dante Alighieri was born in Florence around 1265 into a family of minor nobility. As a boy he met Beatrice Portinari, who became the inspiration of his life's work even though he married Gemma Donati and Beatrice married another man and died young in 1290. He studied philosophy and rhetoric, wrote love poetry in the new sweet style, and gathered his early poems with prose commentary in the Vita Nuova. He entered Florentine politics on the side of the White Guelphs and served as one of the city's priors in 1300. In 1302, while away on an embassy to Rome, he was condemned and exiled by the victorious Black faction. He never returned, living at courts in Verona and elsewhere, and died in Ravenna in 1321, shortly after finishing the Comedy.

In exile Dante wrote treatises on the vernacular language and on monarchy and above all the Commedia, which later readers called divine. Its scheme is vast and precise: a hundred cantos in interlocking terza rima, a cosmos ordered by number and theology, and hundreds of historical figures judged in the afterlife. By writing it in Tuscan rather than Latin he did more than anyone to create the Italian literary language. Boccaccio lectured on him in Florence, the Romantics rediscovered him, and his visions of Hell in particular have inspired artists from Botticelli and Blake to Doré and Rodin.

name: Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca)
bio: Poet and scholar whose sonnets to Laura set the pattern for European love poetry, and whose passion for classical learning made him the father of humanism.
bio_full: Francesco Petrarca was born in Arezzo in 1304 to a Florentine exile and grew up largely in Avignon, then the seat of the papacy. He studied law at Montpellier and Bologna but abandoned it for letters, taking minor orders that gave him church income. On Good Friday 1327 in Avignon, by his own account, he first saw Laura, the woman his poems celebrate, whose identity is uncertain; she died in the plague of 1348. Petrarch travelled widely, searched monastery libraries for lost classical texts, and in 1341 was crowned poet laureate in Rome. He spent his later years in Milan, Venice and Padua and died at Arquà in 1374.

Petrarch considered his Latin works, including the epic Africa and his many letters, his real legacy, but posterity valued most his Italian poems, the Canzoniere. In them he refined the sonnet and created a vocabulary of love as sweet torment, full of paradox, that poets in Spain, France and England imitated for three centuries. Petrarchism shaped Wyatt, Sidney, Ronsard and Shakespeare. As a scholar he recovered lost works by Cicero, promoted the study of ancient Rome and called the centuries after its fall a dark age, an idea that helped define the Renaissance.

name: Giovanni Boccaccio
bio: Author of the Decameron, a hundred tales told during the Black Death, and a pioneer of Italian prose and humanist scholarship.
bio_full: Giovanni Boccaccio was born in 1313, the illegitimate son of a Florentine merchant, probably in Florence or Certaldo. His father sent him to Naples to learn banking and then canon law, but he spent his time at the cultured Angevin court and began writing poems and romances in Italian. Back in Florence from about 1341, he lived through the plague of 1348, which killed perhaps half the city and provides the frame of the Decameron, completed around 1353. In 1350 he met Petrarch, who became his close friend and turned him towards classical scholarship. In his last years he gave the first public lectures on Dante in Florence. He died at Certaldo in 1375.

The Decameron established Italian prose as a literary medium and the novella as a European form. Boccaccio's tales range from bawdy farce to tragedy and show merchants, clergy, lovers and tricksters with unusual realism and humour. He also wrote vernacular poems that Chaucer used for the Knight's Tale and Troilus and Criseyde, and Latin works such as the Genealogy of the Pagan Gods and On Famous Women, which were standard reference works for centuries. Shakespeare, Chaucer, Keats and Pasolini all drew on him.

name: Geoffrey Chaucer
bio: Often called the father of English literature, the poet of The Canterbury Tales was also a courtier, diplomat and civil servant.
bio_full: Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London in the early 1340s, the son of a prosperous wine merchant. He served as a page in an aristocratic household, was captured while fighting in France in 1359 and ransomed, and went on to a long career in royal service under Edward III and Richard II. He travelled on diplomatic missions to France and Italy, where he encountered the works of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio, served as controller of customs in the port of London and later as clerk of the king's works. He married Philippa Roet, whose sister later married John of Gaunt. He died in 1400 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, the first poet in what became Poets' Corner.

Chaucer wrote in the London English of his day at a time when French and Latin were the languages of prestige, and his success did much to establish English as a literary language. His early works, such as The Book of the Duchess and The Parliament of Fowls, adapt French dream-vision poetry; Troilus and Criseyde transforms Boccaccio into a subtle tragic romance; and The Canterbury Tales presents a whole society in comic and serious stories. He introduced new verse forms, notably rhyme royal and the iambic pentameter couplet, into English. Later poets from Spenser to Dryden revered him as their founder.

name: François Rabelais
bio: Monk, physician and humanist whose comic saga of the giants Gargantua and Pantagruel is one of the great carnivals of European literature.
bio_full: François Rabelais was born around 1494 near Chinon in the Loire valley, the son of a lawyer. He became a Franciscan friar and then a Benedictine, learning Greek at a time when the Sorbonne regarded it with suspicion, and corresponded with the great humanist Guillaume Budé. In the late 1520s he left the cloister, studied medicine at Montpellier and became a physician at the hospital in Lyon, where he edited Hippocrates and Galen. There in 1532 he published Pantagruel under the anagram Alcofribas Nasier, followed by Gargantua in 1534 and three further books. Protected by the powerful du Bellay family, he travelled to Rome several times, and the Sorbonne repeatedly condemned his books. He died in Paris in 1553.

Rabelais's books mix humanist learning with popular humour of the most bodily kind: feasts, drinking, lists, coined words, parodies of scholastic argument and satire of monks, lawyers and theologians. Beneath the comedy is an optimistic humanism, expressed in the utopian Abbey of Thélème, whose only rule is do what you will. His exuberant style enriched the French language with hundreds of words. The Russian critic Mikhail Bakhtin made him the centre of his theory of the carnivalesque, and writers from Swift and Sterne to Joyce acknowledged his influence.

name: Michel de Montaigne
bio: The inventor of the essay, who made the examination of his own mind and habits into a new form of literature and philosophy.
bio_full: Michel Eyquem de Montaigne was born in 1533 at his family's château near Bordeaux, into a wealthy merchant family recently ennobled. His father had him taught Latin as his first language. He studied law and served for thirteen years as a magistrate in the Bordeaux parlement, where he formed an intense friendship with the writer Étienne de La Boétie, whose early death in 1563 marked him deeply. In 1571 he retired to his tower library to read and write, and in 1580 published the first two books of his Essays. He travelled through Germany and Italy, served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux during the Wars of Religion, and kept revising and enlarging the Essays until his death in 1592.

Montaigne called his pieces essais, attempts or trials, and they range freely over subjects from cannibals and friendship to thumbs, cruelty and death, always returning to himself as the one subject he could know. He wrote in a conversational, digressive French, quoting the ancients constantly while doubting all certainty; his motto was What do I know? His sceptical, tolerant humanism influenced Shakespeare, who borrowed from John Florio's 1603 translation, as well as Bacon, Pascal, Descartes and Emerson. The personal essay as a literary form descends from him.

name: Miguel de Cervantes
bio: Soldier, captive, tax collector and the author of Don Quixote, widely regarded as the first modern novel and the greatest work of Spanish literature.
bio_full: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra was born in 1547 at Alcalá de Henares, the son of an impoverished surgeon. As a young man he went to Italy, joined the Spanish army and fought at the naval battle of Lepanto in 1571, where a wound left his left hand useless. Returning to Spain in 1575, his ship was captured by Barbary pirates and he spent five years as a slave in Algiers, attempting escape four times before being ransomed. Back in Spain he wrote plays and a pastoral romance, La Galatea, with little success, and worked as a requisitioner of supplies for the Armada and as a tax collector, landing in prison over irregular accounts. In 1605, at fifty-seven, he published the first part of Don Quixote, which was an immediate success. The second part appeared in 1615, and he died in Madrid in 1616.

Cervantes's genius lies in the play between illusion and reality, the high-flown and the everyday, and in characters who change through conversation. Don Quixote parodies chivalric romances while creating something new: a long prose fiction aware of itself as a book, full of other stories, unreliable narrators and arguments about literature. He also wrote the Exemplary Novels, twelve fine short tales, and the posthumous romance Persiles and Sigismunda. Spanish is often called the language of Cervantes, and novelists from Fielding and Sterne to Dostoevsky, Flaubert and Borges counted him as a master.

name: Christopher Marlowe
bio: The brilliant, short-lived Elizabethan playwright who made blank verse the voice of English drama in Tamburlaine and Doctor Faustus.
bio_full: Christopher Marlowe was born in Canterbury in 1564, the son of a shoemaker, the same year as Shakespeare. He won a scholarship to Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, and when the university hesitated to grant his MA in 1587 the Privy Council intervened, stating that he had done the Queen good service, which has led to the belief that he worked as a government agent. In London he quickly became the leading playwright of the day with Tamburlaine the Great, followed by Doctor Faustus, The Jew of Malta and Edward II. He was accused of atheism, and in May 1593 he was stabbed to death in a house in Deptford, in a quarrel over a bill according to the inquest. The exact circumstances are still debated.

Marlowe transformed the English stage by giving it what Ben Jonson called his mighty line: thundering, sonorous blank verse. His heroes are overreachers who desire limitless power, knowledge or wealth, and his plays explore ambition, religion and transgression with a daring unusual for his time. His narrative poem Hero and Leander and the lyric The Passionate Shepherd to His Love were also widely admired. Shakespeare's early histories and tragedies owe much to him, and some scholars believe the two collaborated on the Henry VI plays.

name: William Shakespeare
bio: Playwright, poet and actor, the most widely performed dramatist in the world and the central figure of English literature.
bio_full: William Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of a glover and town official, and probably attended the local grammar school. At eighteen he married Anne Hathaway, with whom he had three children, including a son, Hamnet, who died at eleven. By 1592 he was established in London as an actor and playwright, and from 1594 he was a member and shareholder of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men, who built the Globe Theatre in 1599. Over about twenty-five years he wrote, alone or with collaborators, some thirty-nine plays, as well as the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece and a sequence of 154 sonnets. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there in 1616. Seven years later, two fellow actors published thirty-six of his plays in the First Folio.

Shakespeare wrote comedies, histories, tragedies and late romances, and in each he extended what the form could do. His characters, from Falstaff and Rosalind to Hamlet, Lear and Cleopatra, speak with an individual inner life that later critics saw as a new representation of human personality. His language is immensely rich, mixing high poetry and colloquial prose, and many of his phrases became part of everyday English. His reputation grew steadily, from Ben Jonson's tribute that he was not of an age but for all time to the Romantic idolatry of the nineteenth century, and his plays are now performed, translated and adapted around the world.

name: Lope de Vega
bio: The astonishingly prolific creator of Spain's national theatre, who claimed to have written some 1,500 plays. Cervantes called him a monster of nature.
bio_full: Félix Lope de Vega y Carpio was born in Madrid in 1562 to a family of modest means and was writing verses before he could write, according to his own account. He studied at Alcalá, took part in a naval expedition to the Azores and sailed with the Armada in 1588. His life was turbulent: he was banished from Madrid for libelling a former lover's family, eloped with another woman, married twice and had many affairs and children. In 1614 he became a priest, but his romantic entanglements continued. Throughout he wrote at enormous speed, poems, novels and above all plays for Madrid's public theatres, which made him the most famous writer in Spain. He died in Madrid in 1635, and his funeral drew huge crowds.

In his verse treatise The New Art of Writing Plays (1609), Lope defended a popular theatre that mixed comedy and tragedy, ignored the classical unities and aimed above all to please the audience. His three-act comedia, written in a variety of verse forms, dealt with honour, love, history and peasant dignity, and established the model followed by Tirso de Molina, Calderón and others. About four hundred of his plays survive, among them Fuenteovejuna, Peribáñez and The Knight of Olmedo, along with a large body of lyric poetry.

name: Pedro Calderón de la Barca
bio: The last great dramatist of the Spanish Golden Age, whose Life Is a Dream turned the comedia into philosophical theatre.
bio_full: Pedro Calderón de la Barca was born in Madrid in 1600 into a family of minor nobility and educated by the Jesuits and at the universities of Alcalá and Salamanca. His first plays were staged in the 1620s, and after Lope de Vega's death in 1635 he became the leading dramatist of Spain and the favourite playwright of Philip IV, writing lavish spectacles for the court theatre at the Buen Retiro palace. He served as a soldier in the Catalan revolt of 1640 and in 1651 was ordained a priest. In later life he wrote mainly autos sacramentales, allegorical religious plays performed at the feast of Corpus Christi. He died in Madrid in 1681.

Calderón refined Lope's popular comedia into a more tightly constructed, intellectual drama, with elaborate imagery and themes of free will, illusion, honour and divine grace. His best-known works include Life Is a Dream, The Mayor of Zalamea, The Physician of His Own Honour and the auto The Great Theatre of the World. He was rediscovered by the German Romantics, especially the Schlegel brothers and Goethe, who placed him alongside Shakespeare, and his work was translated into English by Edward FitzGerald.

name: John Donne
bio: The foremost metaphysical poet, whose love poems and Holy Sonnets argue, joke and agonise in startling images. He ended his life as Dean of St Paul's.
bio_full: John Donne was born in London in 1572 into a Roman Catholic family at a time when Catholics were persecuted; his brother died in prison for harbouring a priest. He studied at Oxford and Cambridge, though as a Catholic he could not take a degree, and at the Inns of Court, and sailed with the Earl of Essex on the raids on Cádiz and the Azores. He became secretary to the Lord Keeper, Sir Thomas Egerton, but his secret marriage in 1601 to Egerton's young niece Anne More cost him his post and briefly his liberty, and years of poverty followed. Having conformed to the Church of England, he was ordained in 1615 at the urging of James I, became a celebrated preacher and was appointed Dean of St Paul's Cathedral in 1621. He died in 1631.

Donne's poems, mostly published after his death in 1633, combine passionate feeling with intricate argument and far-fetched comparisons, the conceits for which Samuel Johnson later named him and his followers the metaphysical poets. His Songs and Sonnets range from cynical wit to intense devotion, and his Holy Sonnets wrestle with death and salvation. His sermons and Devotions upon Emergent Occasions are among the finest English prose of the age. Neglected in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, he was championed by T. S. Eliot and the modernists and is now one of the most admired English poets.

name: John Milton
bio: Poet and polemicist of the English Revolution, author of Paradise Lost, the great epic of the Fall written after he had gone blind.
bio_full: John Milton was born in London in 1608, the son of a prosperous scrivener and composer. He studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, and then spent years of private study, writing early masterpieces such as the masque Comus and the elegy Lycidas, before travelling in Italy, where he met the aged Galileo. During the conflict between King and Parliament he wrote pamphlets on church reform, divorce and, in Areopagitica (1644), freedom of the press. After the execution of Charles I he defended the regicide and served the Commonwealth as Secretary for Foreign Tongues. By 1652 he was completely blind. At the Restoration in 1660 he was briefly imprisoned and lived thereafter in retirement, dictating Paradise Lost (1667), Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes. He died in 1674.

Milton aimed to write an epic in English to rival Homer and Virgil, and in Paradise Lost he did, in a grand, Latinate blank verse of immense learning and musical power. His treatment of Satan, whom Blake said Milton portrayed as being of the Devil's party without knowing it, has fascinated readers ever since. A fierce defender of liberty of conscience, he influenced political thought as well as poetry. Wordsworth, Blake, Shelley and Keats all wrestled with his example, and he remains, with Shakespeare, a central figure of English literature.

name: Molière (Jean-Baptiste Poquelin)
bio: Actor, manager and France's greatest comic playwright, whose Tartuffe, The Misanthrope and The Miser created the comedy of character.
bio_full: Jean-Baptiste Poquelin was born in Paris in 1622, the son of a prosperous upholsterer to the royal household. Educated by the Jesuits, he gave up a secure future to found a theatre company in 1643 with the actress Madeleine Béjart, taking the stage name Molière. After the company's failure in Paris he spent thirteen years touring the provinces, learning his craft from Italian commedia dell'arte. Back in Paris from 1658, he won the patronage of Louis XIV and wrote a stream of comedies, including The School for Wives, Tartuffe, Don Juan, The Misanthrope, The Miser and The Bourgeois Gentleman. His attacks on hypocrisy provoked powerful enemies; Tartuffe was banned for five years. He collapsed while playing the title role of The Imaginary Invalid in 1673 and died a few hours later.

Molière combined the physical comedy of farce with sharp observation of social types, the hypocrite, the miser, the snob, the hypochondriac, the pedant and the jealous husband, and made laughter a means of moral and social criticism. Many of his plays are written in elegant alexandrine couplets. The Comédie-Française, founded in 1680 from his company, is still called the House of Molière, and French is sometimes called the language of Molière. He is among the most performed playwrights in the world.

name: Jean Racine
bio: The master of French classical tragedy, whose Andromaque and Phèdre distil overwhelming passion into perfectly controlled verse.
bio_full: Jean Racine was born in 1639 at La Ferté-Milon and orphaned young. He was educated at the Jansenist abbey of Port-Royal, where he learned Greek and absorbed a severe Augustinian view of human weakness. Moving to Paris, he turned to the theatre, to the dismay of his teachers, and after early plays staged by Molière's company he achieved his first triumph with Andromaque in 1667. Over the next ten years he wrote Britannicus, Bérénice, Bajazet, Mithridate, Iphigénie and Phèdre (1677). Then he abruptly withdrew from the public theatre, married, reconciled with Port-Royal and became royal historiographer to Louis XIV. He returned to drama only for two biblical plays, Esther and Athalie, written for a girls' school at Saint-Cyr. He died in 1699.

Racine's tragedies observe the classical unities and use a small vocabulary and the twelve-syllable alexandrine with extraordinary musical precision. Within these strict limits, his characters, especially his women, are consumed by love, jealousy and guilt, and their fate unfolds with relentless logic. Where Corneille celebrated the will, Racine showed passion overwhelming it. He is regarded as the greatest French tragedian, and his plays remain central to the repertory of the Comédie-Française.

name: Daniel Defoe
bio: Merchant, spy, pamphleteer and journalist who in his late fifties wrote Robinson Crusoe, one of the founding works of the English novel.
bio_full: Daniel Foe, who later added the aristocratic-sounding De to his name, was born in London around 1660, the son of a Dissenting tallow chandler. Educated at a Dissenting academy, he became a merchant in hosiery, wine and other goods, took part in Monmouth's rebellion of 1685 and went bankrupt more than once. He wrote hundreds of pamphlets on politics, trade and religion; one satire, The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702), led to his being pilloried and imprisoned. He then worked as a secret agent and propagandist for the government, notably in Scotland during the negotiations for the Union of 1707, and wrote almost single-handed a periodical, the Review. In 1719 he published Robinson Crusoe, followed by Moll Flanders, A Journal of the Plague Year and Roxana. He died in London in 1731.

Defoe's fiction presents itself as the true account of real people, told in plain, circumstantial prose full of practical detail, accounts and lists. This documentary realism, applied to the lives of ordinary or marginal people, a castaway, a thief, a courtesan, made him one of the founders of the English novel. His interest in trade, work and individual self-reliance has led critics to see his books as expressions of a new economic outlook. Robinson Crusoe has never been out of print and has been imitated so often that castaway stories are called Robinsonades.

name: Jonathan Swift
bio: The greatest satirist in English, author of Gulliver's Travels and A Modest Proposal, and Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin.
bio_full: Jonathan Swift was born in Dublin in 1667 to English parents, his father having died before his birth. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and became secretary to the statesman Sir William Temple in England, where he met Esther Johnson, the Stella of his later letters. Ordained in the Church of Ireland, he made his name with A Tale of a Tub (1704), a satire on religious excess. In London he became a leading writer for the Tory government of 1710–14 and a friend of Pope, Gay and Arbuthnot in the Scriblerus Club. On the fall of the Tories he became Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, where he spent the rest of his life and became a hero to the Irish for his attacks on English policy, notably in the Drapier's Letters. Gulliver's Travels appeared in 1726. In his last years he suffered severe illness, and he died in 1745.

Swift's satire works through a deadpan persona, an earnest narrator who calmly reports or proposes absurdities, leaving the reader to recognise the horror. His targets were pride, cruelty, corruption, scientific and religious folly and the oppression of Ireland. His prose is plain, exact and devastating. Swift left money to found a hospital for the mentally ill, and his own epitaph, which he composed in Latin, speaks of the savage indignation that tore his heart. Gulliver's Travels has become both a classic of satire and, in shortened form, a children's book.

name: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
bio: The most famous writer of the French Enlightenment, a tireless campaigner against intolerance whose satirical tale Candide is still widely read.
bio_full: François-Marie Arouet was born in Paris in 1694, the son of a notary, and educated by the Jesuits. His sharp verses landed him in the Bastille in 1717, where he adopted the name Voltaire, and his tragedy Oedipe made him famous the next year. After a quarrel with an aristocrat he was exiled to England (1726–28), where he admired the freedom of thought, Newton and Locke, and described it all in his Philosophical Letters, which were burned in Paris. He lived for years with the scientist Émilie du Châtelet at Cirey, spent an uneasy period at the court of Frederick the Great in Prussia and finally settled at Ferney, near the Swiss border, where he campaigned against judicial injustice, notably in the case of Jean Calas. He returned to Paris in triumph in 1778 and died there that year.

Voltaire wrote in almost every genre: tragedies, epic poetry, history, philosophy, tales and more than twenty thousand letters. His philosophical tales, especially Candide, Zadig and Micromégas, use irony and swift, lucid prose to ridicule dogma, superstition and complacent optimism. His slogan, crush the infamous thing, was aimed at religious fanaticism and persecution. More than any other writer he made the ideas of the Enlightenment, tolerance, reason and freedom of expression, fashionable throughout Europe, and his remains were moved to the Panthéon during the Revolution.

name: Laurence Sterne
bio: A Yorkshire clergyman whose Tristram Shandy, a novel of digressions, black pages and missing chapters, made him a celebrity and a forerunner of modern experimental fiction.
bio_full: Laurence Sterne was born in 1713 at Clonmel in Ireland, the son of an English army officer, and spent his childhood moving between garrisons. He was educated at Jesus College, Cambridge, was ordained, and for over twenty years was a country parson near York, unhappily married and little known. In 1759 he published the first two volumes of The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman, which caused a sensation in London; seven more volumes followed until 1767. Suffering from tuberculosis, he travelled in France and Italy for his health, an experience he turned into A Sentimental Journey through France and Italy (1768). He died in London weeks after it appeared.

Sterne built his comedy on the idea, taken from John Locke, that the mind works by chance associations. His narrator can barely get himself born, wanders into endless digressions and plays with the printed page itself. Combined with a warm, sentimental humour, this made Sterne immensely popular across Europe; Goethe, Diderot and Pushkin admired him. In the twentieth century, writers and critics recognised in Tristram Shandy techniques of modernism and postmodernism, and the Russian formalist Viktor Shklovsky called it the most typical novel in world literature.

name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
bio: Philosopher, novelist and autobiographer whose Julie and Confessions taught Europe a new language of feeling, nature and the self.
bio_full: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712; his mother died days after his birth, and he left the city at sixteen to begin a wandering life. He found a protector in Madame de Warens in Savoy, then went to Paris, where he worked as a music copyist, wrote an opera and contributed to the Encyclopédie. His Discourse on the Sciences and Arts (1750) made him famous with its argument that civilisation corrupts. His epistolary novel Julie, or the New Heloise (1761) was one of the best-selling books of the century, and Emile and The Social Contract followed in 1762. Both were condemned, and he spent years in flight and growing persecution mania, staying for a time in England with David Hume. He wrote his autobiographical Confessions and Reveries of the Solitary Walker in his last years and died near Paris in 1778.

Rousseau's influence on politics and education belongs to philosophy, but his literary impact was just as great. Julie fused a love story with descriptions of Alpine nature and moral reflection, and readers responded with tears and letters. The Confessions, which open by promising to show a man in all the truth of nature, founded modern autobiography. His cult of sincerity, sensibility and the natural world prepared the ground for Romanticism, and writers from Goethe and Wordsworth to Tolstoy acknowledged him as a liberator.

name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
bio: Poet, dramatist, novelist, scientist and statesman, the towering figure of German literature and author of Faust.
bio_full: Johann Wolfgang Goethe was born in Frankfurt in 1749 into a wealthy family and studied law at Leipzig and Strasbourg, where Herder introduced him to Shakespeare, folk song and Gothic architecture. His drama Götz von Berlichingen (1773) and the novel The Sorrows of Young Werther (1774) made him the leader of the Sturm und Drang and a European celebrity at twenty-five. In 1775 he accepted an invitation from Duke Karl August to Weimar, where he spent the rest of his life as minister, theatre director and court poet. A journey to Italy in 1786–88 turned him towards classicism. His friendship with Schiller from 1794 until Schiller's death in 1805 was one of the great literary partnerships. He worked on Faust for some sixty years, completing the second part shortly before his death in Weimar in 1832.

Goethe's output is vast: lyric poetry of every kind, plays such as Iphigenia in Tauris and Torquato Tasso, the novels Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship, the founding Bildungsroman, and Elective Affinities, an autobiography and scientific works on plant metamorphosis and the theory of colour. He coined the idea of world literature. Many of his poems were set by Schubert, Schumann and Wolf, and Faust inspired operas by Gounod and Berlioz. For Germans he occupies a position comparable to Shakespeare's for the English, and Napoleon, meeting him, is said to have exclaimed that here was a man.

name: William Blake
bio: Visionary poet, painter and printmaker who etched and coloured his own illuminated books, from Songs of Innocence and of Experience to his prophetic epics.
bio_full: William Blake was born in London in 1757, the son of a hosier, and apprenticed at fourteen to the engraver James Basire. He studied briefly at the Royal Academy, married Catherine Boucher, who became his collaborator, and worked all his life as a commercial engraver. From childhood he reported visions of angels and spirits. In 1788 he developed a method of relief etching that let him print text and image together, which he used for Songs of Innocence (1789), Songs of Experience (1794) and a series of prophetic books including The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Milton and Jerusalem. He spent three years in Felpham on the Sussex coast and was tried, and acquitted, for sedition in 1804. He lived and died in poverty in London in 1827, admired by a small circle of young artists.

Blake's poetry ranges from the simple-seeming lyrics of the Songs to dense mythological epics populated by his own invented beings, such as Urizen and Los. He attacked rationalism, repressive religion, slavery and the industrial and social conditions of his day, and believed in the imagination as the divine in humanity. Little known in his lifetime, he was rediscovered by the Pre-Raphaelites and Yeats, and his lyrics, such as The Tyger and the verses known as Jerusalem, are now among the best known in English.

name: William Wordsworth
bio: The central poet of English Romanticism, who made memory, nature and ordinary life the subject of great poetry. Poet Laureate from 1843.
bio_full: William Wordsworth was born in 1770 in Cockermouth in the Lake District and lost both parents as a boy. He studied at St John's College, Cambridge, and in 1790–92 travelled in revolutionary France, where he was swept up in republican enthusiasm and fathered a daughter with Annette Vallon. War between Britain and France separated them, and the Terror disillusioned him. From 1795 he lived with his sister Dorothy, whose journals often inspired his poems, and formed a close friendship with Coleridge, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads in 1798. In 1799 he settled at Dove Cottage in Grasmere, married Mary Hutchinson and later moved to Rydal Mount. His political views became conservative, and he succeeded Southey as Poet Laureate in 1843. He died in 1850; his great autobiographical poem The Prelude was published that year.

In the preface to Lyrical Ballads, Wordsworth called for poetry in the real language of men and defined poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, recollected in tranquillity. His best work, written roughly between 1797 and 1807, explores the growth of the mind, childhood memory and the healing power of landscape, in poems such as Tintern Abbey, the Immortality Ode and The Prelude. He changed what English poetry could be about and influenced not only later poets but also the way people value nature and wilderness.

name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
bio: Poet, critic and philosopher, co-author with Wordsworth of Lyrical Ballads and creator of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan.
bio_full: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was born in 1772 at Ottery St Mary in Devon, the youngest son of a vicar, and educated at Christ's Hospital in London and Jesus College, Cambridge, which he left without a degree after briefly enlisting in the dragoons under a false name. With Robert Southey he planned an ideal community in America that never materialised. In 1797 he settled near Wordsworth in Somerset, and their year of intense collaboration produced Lyrical Ballads, which opened with his Rime of the Ancient Mariner. He studied philosophy in Germany, moved to the Lake District, and struggled for most of his adult life with opium addiction and an unhappy marriage. From 1816 he lived in Highgate in the house of the physician James Gillman, where he became a famous talker and sage. He died there in 1834.

Coleridge's poetic output is small but includes some of the most haunting poems in English: the Ancient Mariner, Christabel, Kubla Khan and the conversation poems such as Frost at Midnight. As a critic he was equally important. His Biographia Literaria (1817) and lectures on Shakespeare introduced German Romantic philosophy to Britain, distinguished imagination from fancy, and gave the phrase the willing suspension of disbelief. He shaped how the nineteenth century thought about poetry, religion and the state.

name: Jane Austen
bio: The novelist of English country society whose six novels, including Pride and Prejudice and Emma, combine sharp irony with deep moral seriousness.
bio_full: Jane Austen was born in 1775 at Steventon in Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a country clergyman. She was educated mainly at home, in a lively, bookish family that staged plays and read novels aloud, and began writing comic pieces as a girl. She never married; she accepted a proposal in 1802 but withdrew her consent the next day. After her father's retirement the family lived in Bath and Southampton, and in 1809 she settled with her mother and sister Cassandra in a cottage at Chawton provided by her brother Edward. There she revised and published Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815), all anonymously. She fell ill in 1816 and died in Winchester in 1817. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death.

Austen limited herself, as she said, to three or four families in a country village, and within that world she examined money, marriage, class and moral judgement with exactness and wit. She perfected free indirect discourse, which lets the narrative voice slip in and out of a character's thoughts, giving readers both sympathy and ironic distance. Her reputation grew slowly through the nineteenth century and then enormously in the twentieth, through scholarship, a devoted readership and countless film and television adaptations. She is now among the most widely read novelists in English.

name: Lord Byron (George Gordon Byron)
bio: The most famous poet of his age, whose brooding heroes and scandalous life created the Byronic legend. He died supporting Greek independence.
bio_full: George Gordon Byron was born in London in 1788, with a deformed right foot, and inherited his great-uncle's title at ten. Educated at Harrow and Trinity College, Cambridge, he travelled through Portugal, Spain, Albania and Greece in 1809–11, and the first two cantos of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, based on these travels, made him famous overnight in 1812. A string of affairs, debts and a short, disastrous marriage to Annabella Milbanke, together with rumours of incest with his half-sister Augusta, drove him from England in 1816, never to return. In Switzerland he spent a summer with Percy and Mary Shelley; in Italy he lived in Venice, Ravenna and Pisa and wrote his comic masterpiece Don Juan. In 1823 he went to Greece to support the war of independence against the Ottomans and died of fever at Missolonghi in 1824.

Byron created the Byronic hero, proud, melancholy, guilty and defiant, a figure who fascinated Europe and influenced Pushkin, Lermontov, Delacroix, Berlioz and countless others. Yet his greatest achievement is arguably the comic, conversational and satirical Don Juan, written in ottava rima with brilliant rhymes and digressions. He was admired abroad perhaps even more than at home, and his death made him a national hero in Greece. His daughter Ada Lovelace became a pioneer of computing.

name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
bio: Radical Romantic poet of Ozymandias, Ode to the West Wind and Prometheus Unbound, who drowned off the Italian coast at twenty-nine.
bio_full: Percy Bysshe Shelley was born in 1792 into a wealthy Sussex family and educated at Eton and University College, Oxford, from which he was expelled in 1811 for co-writing a pamphlet titled The Necessity of Atheism. That year he eloped with sixteen-year-old Harriet Westbrook. In 1814 he left her for Mary Godwin, daughter of the philosopher William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, and they married in 1816 after Harriet's suicide. Ostracised in England and denied custody of his children, Shelley moved to Italy in 1818, where he wrote most of his major works, including Prometheus Unbound, The Cenci, Ode to the West Wind and Adonais, an elegy for Keats. In July 1822 his boat sank in a storm in the Gulf of La Spezia, and he drowned. His body was cremated on the beach near Viareggio.

Shelley was a political radical, vegetarian and atheist who believed poetry could change the world; his Defence of Poetry ends by calling poets the unacknowledged legislators of the world. His verse is musical, rapid and abstract, full of images of wind, light, clouds and fire, and his political poems, such as The Mask of Anarchy, were later read by Chartists and campaigners for non-violent protest. Long condemned as immoral, he was championed by the Victorians as a lyric genius and remains one of the major English Romantic poets.

name: Mary Shelley
bio: Author of Frankenstein, begun at nineteen during a ghost-story contest with Byron and Percy Shelley, and a founding work of science fiction.
bio_full: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London in 1797, the daughter of the philosopher William Godwin and the feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days after her birth. She grew up among her father's intellectual circle, and at sixteen eloped to the Continent with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, whom she married in 1816. That summer, near Geneva with Byron and his physician John Polidori, she conceived the story that became Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818. The following years in Italy were marked by the deaths of three of her four children and, in 1822, of Shelley himself. Returning to England with her surviving son, she supported herself by writing novels, including The Last Man (1826), stories, travel writing and biographies, and edited Shelley's poems. She died in London in 1851.

Frankenstein combines the Gothic novel with Romantic ideas about creation, ambition and the outcast, and with contemporary science about galvanism and the origins of life. Its framing of nested narratives and the eloquent voice of the creature give it unusual depth. The novel has had an enormous afterlife on stage and screen and is often called the first true work of science fiction. The Last Man, a story of humanity destroyed by plague, is also now regarded as a pioneering work of the genre.

name: John Keats
bio: The Romantic poet of the great odes, who wrote almost all his major work in a few years before dying of tuberculosis at twenty-five.
bio_full: John Keats was born in London in 1795, the son of a livery-stable keeper; his father died when he was eight and his mother when he was fourteen. He trained as a surgeon at Guy's Hospital and qualified as an apothecary, but gave up medicine for poetry. Leigh Hunt published his early sonnets, including On First Looking into Chapman's Homer, and his first collection appeared in 1817, followed by the long poem Endymion (1818), which hostile reviewers mocked. In 1818 he nursed his brother Tom through his fatal tuberculosis and fell in love with Fanny Brawne. In an astonishing burst in 1819 he wrote The Eve of St Agnes, La Belle Dame sans Merci, the great odes and Hyperion. Already ill with tuberculosis, he travelled to Rome for his health in 1820 and died there in February 1821.

Keats's poetry is famed for its sensuous imagery, its rich music and its meditation on beauty, mortality and art. His letters, full of ideas such as negative capability, the capacity to rest in uncertainty without reaching after fact and reason, are among the finest by any English poet. His short life became a Romantic legend, fixed by Shelley's elegy Adonais, and the Victorians, the Pre-Raphaelites and later poets made him one of the best loved of all English poets.

name: Alexander Pushkin
bio: The founder of modern Russian literature, author of Eugene Onegin and The Bronze Horseman, killed in a duel at thirty-seven.
bio_full: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was born in Moscow in 1799 into an old noble family; his maternal great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, had been brought to Russia as an African child and became a general under Peter the Great. Educated at the new lycée at Tsarskoye Selo, he was already a celebrated poet when he graduated. His political verses led to exile in the south of Russia in 1820 and then to confinement on his mother's estate at Mikhailovskoye. Pardoned by Nicholas I in 1826, he remained under the tsar's personal censorship. He married the beautiful Natalya Goncharova in 1831. Rumours of an affair between her and the French officer Georges d'Anthès led Pushkin to challenge him to a duel in January 1837, in which he was mortally wounded.

Pushkin wrote lyric poems, narrative poems, the novel in verse Eugene Onegin, the historical drama Boris Godunov, the Little Tragedies, prose tales such as The Queen of Spades and the historical novel The Captain's Daughter. He fused the Russian vernacular with the literary language and achieved a clarity, lightness and range that made him the foundation on which Gogol, Lermontov, Tolstoy and Dostoevsky built. Many of his works became operas by Glinka, Mussorgsky and Tchaikovsky. In Russia he is regarded as the national poet, beyond comparison.

portrait_caption: Orest Kiprensky, Alexander Pushkin, 1827, Tretyakov Gallery

name: Victor Hugo
bio: The giant of French Romanticism, poet, dramatist and novelist of Notre-Dame de Paris and Les Misérables, and a republican exile under Napoleon III.
bio_full: Victor-Marie Hugo was born in Besançon in 1802, the son of an officer in Napoleon's army, and spent part of his childhood in Italy and Spain. He published his first collection of odes at twenty and soon led the young Romantics. The preface to his play Cromwell (1827) was their manifesto, and the riotous premiere of Hernani in 1830 marked their victory over classicism. Notre-Dame de Paris appeared in 1831. The drowning of his daughter Léopoldine in 1843 devastated him. Elected to the Assembly, he opposed Louis-Napoleon's coup of 1851 and went into exile for nearly twenty years, mainly on Guernsey, where he wrote Les Contemplations, The Legend of the Ages and Les Misérables. He returned to Paris in 1870 as a national symbol and died in 1885; some two million people attended his funeral and burial in the Panthéon.

Hugo's work is enormous in scale and range: lyric and epic poetry, verse drama, novels, essays, political speeches and some four thousand drawings. He championed the mixing of the sublime and the grotesque, sympathy for the poor and the outcast, and campaigns against the death penalty and for universal education. His novels have become global myths through stage musicals and films, while in France he is remembered above all as the greatest poet of the nineteenth century.

portrait_caption: Léon Bonnat, Victor Hugo, 1879

name: Honoré de Balzac
bio: The tireless creator of La Comédie humaine, a cycle of nearly a hundred novels and stories that portrays the whole of French society after Napoleon.
bio_full: Honoré Balzac, who added the aristocratic de himself, was born in Tours in 1799 and sent to a harsh boarding school, then trained in law in Paris. Determined to be a writer, he produced potboiler novels under pseudonyms and lost heavily in ventures as a publisher and printer, leaving debts that pursued him all his life. His first success under his own name was The Chouans (1829), and over the next twenty years he wrote at a ferocious pace, often through the night fuelled by coffee. In 1842 he gathered his novels under the title La Comédie humaine. He conducted a long correspondence and affair with the Polish countess Ewelina Hańska, whom he finally married in 1850, a few months before his death in Paris.

Balzac's innovation was to link his novels through recurring characters, so that bankers, journalists, courtesans, criminals and provincial families reappear across books and form a vast fictional society. He described rooms, money, clothes and ambitions in minute detail, convinced that environment shapes people as it shapes animal species. His masterpieces include Eugénie Grandet, Père Goriot, Lost Illusions and Cousin Bette. Marx and Engels said they learned more about French society from him than from the historians, and novelists from Zola to Proust learned from his method.

portrait_caption: Louis Boulanger, Honoré de Balzac, 1836

name: Nikolai Gogol
bio: The grotesque comic genius of Russian literature, author of The Government Inspector, The Overcoat and Dead Souls.
bio_full: Nikolai Vasilyevich Gogol was born in 1809 in the village of Sorochyntsi in the Poltava region of Ukraine, into a family of minor gentry. He moved to Saint Petersburg in 1828, failed as a civil servant, actor and history lecturer, and found fame with Evenings on a Farm near Dikanka (1831–32), stories of Ukrainian folk life admired by Pushkin. His comedy The Government Inspector (1836), a satire on provincial corruption, was approved by Nicholas I himself but caused uproar. Gogol spent much of the following decade in Rome, where he wrote Dead Souls, published in 1842. In later years he fell under the influence of a fanatical priest, burned the manuscript of the second part of Dead Souls and starved himself, dying in Moscow in 1852.

Gogol's world is absurd, fantastic and pathetic at once: a nose that leaves its owner's face, a poor clerk who dies for the loss of an overcoat, a swindler buying the names of dead serfs. His prose, full of digressions, odd details and verbal fireworks, combines satire with a deep sense of the strangeness of reality. Dostoevsky is said to have remarked that the Russian writers all came out from under Gogol's overcoat, and Nabokov, Bulgakov and Kafka have been compared with him.

name: Edgar Allan Poe
bio: Poet, critic and master of the macabre tale, who invented the modern detective story and profoundly influenced French Symbolism.
bio_full: Edgar Poe was born in Boston in 1809 to travelling actors; his father deserted the family and his mother died when he was two. He was taken in by John Allan, a Richmond merchant, whose name he added to his own, though he was never formally adopted. He studied briefly at the University of Virginia, enlisted in the army and was expelled from West Point. He published his first poems in 1827 and spent the rest of his life as a struggling magazine editor and critic in Richmond, Philadelphia and New York. In 1836 he married his thirteen-year-old cousin Virginia Clemm, who died of tuberculosis in 1847. The Raven (1845) made him famous but not prosperous. He died in Baltimore in 1849 in mysterious circumstances, having been found delirious in the street.

Poe believed that a poem or tale should produce a single unified effect, and his stories of terror, such as The Fall of the House of Usher, The Tell-Tale Heart and The Cask of Amontillado, are tightly built to do so. In The Murders in the Rue Morgue (1841) he created the first fictional detective, C. Auguste Dupin, and he also pioneered science fiction. Baudelaire translated him and Mallarmé and Valéry revered him, so that Poe's influence on French poetry was greater than in his own country. Through Conan Doyle, Lovecraft and horror film he remains one of the most popular American writers.

name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
bio: The novelist of New England's Puritan past, whose The Scarlet Letter explores sin, guilt and hypocrisy.
bio_full: Nathaniel Hathorne, who later added a w to his name, was born in Salem, Massachusetts, in 1804; one of his ancestors had been a judge in the Salem witch trials. He studied at Bowdoin College alongside Longfellow and the future president Franklin Pierce, then spent a decade in near seclusion in Salem writing tales, published as Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He briefly joined the utopian community of Brook Farm, married the painter Sophia Peabody, and worked at the Boston and Salem custom houses. The Scarlet Letter (1850) made his name and was followed by The House of the Seven Gables and The Blithedale Romance. His friend Pierce appointed him consul in Liverpool, and he later lived in Italy. He died in 1864 while travelling in New Hampshire.

Hawthorne called his novels romances, meaning that they mixed realism with symbol, allegory and the supernatural to probe moral and psychological truth. Ambiguous symbols, such as the scarlet A, the minister's black veil or the birthmark, are at the heart of his tales, and his recurring concerns are hidden guilt, pride and the legacy of the Puritan past. Melville dedicated Moby-Dick to him, and Henry James wrote a study of him. He is a founding figure of American fiction.

portrait_caption: Charles Osgood, Nathaniel Hawthorne, 1840, Peabody Essex Museum

name: Charlotte Brontë
bio: Author of Jane Eyre, the eldest of the three Brontë sisters who wrote in a remote Yorkshire parsonage.
bio_full: Charlotte Brontë was born in 1816 at Thornton in Yorkshire, the third of six children of the Irish-born clergyman Patrick Brontë, who moved the family to the parsonage at Haworth on the moors. Her mother died in 1821 and her two elder sisters died of tuberculosis contracted at a harsh boarding school, which she later portrayed as Lowood in Jane Eyre. With her siblings Branwell, Emily and Anne she invented elaborate imaginary kingdoms in childhood writings. She worked as a teacher and governess and studied in Brussels, where she fell unhappily in love with her married teacher Constantin Héger. In 1846 the sisters published a joint volume of poems as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, and in 1847 Jane Eyre became a sensation. Within two years Branwell, Emily and Anne were dead. She wrote Shirley and Villette, married her father's curate Arthur Bell Nicholls in 1854 and died in pregnancy in 1855.

Charlotte Brontë gave the English novel an intense first-person voice of female passion, independence and moral conviction, set against the constraints of class and gender. Her novels draw on Gothic and Romantic elements but are rooted in sharply observed experience. Elizabeth Gaskell's biography of her (1857) created the legend of the Brontës, and Jane Eyre has inspired countless adaptations and responses, notably Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea, which retells the story of Rochester's first wife.

portrait_caption: Charlotte Brontë, from the group portrait by her brother Branwell, c. 1834

name: Emily Brontë
bio: The poet and novelist of Wuthering Heights, a single novel of wild passion on the Yorkshire moors. She died at thirty.
bio_full: Emily Jane Brontë was born at Thornton in Yorkshire in 1818 and grew up at Haworth parsonage, which she left only briefly, for school, a few months as a teacher near Halifax and a period studying in Brussels with Charlotte in 1842. With her younger sister Anne she created the imaginary kingdom of Gondal, the setting of many of her poems. She was reserved and fiercely independent, devoted to the moors and to her animals. Her poems appeared in the sisters' joint collection of 1846 under the name Ellis Bell, and Wuthering Heights was published in December 1847. She caught a cold at the funeral of her brother Branwell in September 1848, refused medical help and died of tuberculosis that December.

Wuthering Heights puzzled and shocked its first reviewers with its violence, its intricate nested narration and the elemental love between Catherine and Heathcliff. It is now considered one of the greatest English novels, a work that fuses Romantic intensity with a rigorous structure. Emily's poems, with their visionary independence and stoicism, are also highly regarded; Emily Dickinson admired them and asked for No coward soul is mine to be read at her funeral.

name: Charles Dickens
bio: The most popular novelist of the Victorian age, creator of Oliver Twist, Scrooge, David Copperfield and a gallery of unforgettable characters.
bio_full: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born in Portsmouth in 1812, the son of a navy pay clerk who was imprisoned for debt in 1824; the twelve-year-old Charles was sent to work in a blacking factory, an experience he never forgot. He became a law clerk and then a parliamentary reporter, and published sketches of London life under the name Boz. The Pickwick Papers (1836–37), issued in monthly parts, made him a phenomenon at twenty-five. Over the next three decades he wrote fifteen novels, including Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol, David Copperfield, Bleak House, Little Dorrit, A Tale of Two Cities and Great Expectations, while editing magazines and campaigning on social issues. He separated from his wife Catherine in 1858, gave hugely popular public readings in Britain and America, and died at his home near Rochester in 1870, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.

Dickens's novels combine comedy, melodrama, satire and social protest, and are populated by grotesque and vivid characters with memorable names and speech. Published in instalments, they reached an enormous public, and he used them to attack the workhouse, debtors' prisons, the law's delays and the exploitation of children. His imaginative vision of London, fog, crowds and all, shaped how the city was seen. Dostoevsky, Kafka and many later writers admired him, and his stories have been adapted for stage and screen more than those of almost any other novelist.

name: Herman Melville
bio: Sailor, novelist and poet whose Moby-Dick, ignored in his lifetime, is now regarded as one of the greatest American novels.
bio_full: Herman Melville was born in New York in 1819 into a distinguished family whose fortunes collapsed with his father's bankruptcy and death in 1832. After working as a clerk and teacher, he went to sea, first on a merchant ship to Liverpool and in 1841 on the whaler Acushnet to the Pacific. He deserted in the Marquesas, lived for a time among the islanders, and returned home by way of Tahiti and Hawaii. His novels based on these adventures, Typee (1846) and Omoo, were popular successes. He married, settled on a farm near Pittsfield, Massachusetts, where he befriended Hawthorne, and wrote Moby-Dick (1851), which sold poorly. Later works, including Pierre, Bartleby and The Confidence-Man, fared worse. From 1866 he worked for nineteen years as a customs inspector in New York, writing poetry in obscurity, and died in 1891, leaving the manuscript of Billy Budd.

Melville moved from adventure narrative to metaphysical inquiry, combining the facts of whaling and seafaring with Shakespearean drama, philosophical speculation and dark questioning of God and fate. He was all but forgotten at his death, and the Melville revival of the 1920s, which began on the centenary of his birth, transformed him into a central figure of American literature. His short works Bartleby, the Scrivener and Benito Cereno are also classics, and Billy Budd was published only in 1924.

name: Walt Whitman
birthplace: West Hills, Long Island, New York
bio: The poet of Leaves of Grass, who celebrated democracy, the body and the self in a sweeping free verse that changed poetry.
bio_full: Walter Whitman was born in 1819 at West Hills on Long Island and grew up in Brooklyn, leaving school at eleven. He worked as a printer, teacher, journalist and editor of several newspapers, including the Brooklyn Daily Eagle. In 1855 he self-published the first edition of Leaves of Grass, twelve untitled poems with his portrait in workman's clothes in place of a name on the title page. Emerson greeted it as the beginning of a great career. Whitman revised and expanded the book for the rest of his life, through nine editions. During the Civil War he worked in Washington as a government clerk and volunteered daily in military hospitals, an experience reflected in Drum-Taps and his elegies for Lincoln. After a stroke in 1873 he settled in Camden, New Jersey, where he died in 1892.

Whitman abandoned rhyme and regular metre for long, rolling lines built on repetition and catalogues, drawing on the rhythms of the Bible and oratory. His poems embrace all of America, its workers, cities, landscapes and contradictions, and speak frankly of the body and sexuality, which made the book notorious. He has been read as the poet of American democracy and as a pioneer voice of same-sex love. Nearly every later American poet has defined themselves in relation to him, and his influence spread to poets as different as Pessoa, Neruda and Ginsberg.

name: Gustave Flaubert
bio: The perfectionist author of Madame Bovary, who made the novel an art of style and impersonal observation.
bio_full: Gustave Flaubert was born in Rouen in 1821, the son of the chief surgeon of the city's hospital. Sent to Paris to study law, he suffered an epileptic-type seizure in 1844 and gave up his studies to live with his mother at the family house at Croisset on the Seine, where he spent most of his life writing. He travelled through Egypt and the Middle East in 1849–51 with his friend Maxime Du Camp. Madame Bovary was serialised in 1856, and he and its publishers were prosecuted for offending public morals; their acquittal in 1857 made the book a bestseller. He went on to write Salammbô, a novel of ancient Carthage, Sentimental Education (1869), The Temptation of Saint Anthony and Three Tales. He was a mentor to Maupassant and friend of George Sand and Turgenev, and died at Croisset in 1880, leaving Bouvard and Pécuchet unfinished.

Flaubert sought what he called le mot juste, the exact word, and laboured for days over single pages, reading his sentences aloud in what he called his shouting room. He believed the author should be present everywhere in the work but visible nowhere, and his impersonal, ironic narration and use of free indirect style became central techniques of the modern novel. Henry James, Joyce, Kafka and Nabokov all revered him. His letters, full of ideas about art and contempt for bourgeois stupidity, are among the great literary correspondences.
