portrait_caption: Eugène Giraud, Gustave Flaubert, c. 1856

name: Charles Baudelaire
bio: Poet of Les Fleurs du mal and the prose poems of Paris Spleen, art critic and translator of Poe, often called the first modern poet.
bio_full: Charles Baudelaire was born in Paris in 1821. His father died when he was six, and his mother married an army officer, General Aupick, whom Charles resented. Expelled from school and leading a bohemian life, he was sent on a voyage towards India in 1841 but turned back at Mauritius and Réunion. On coming of age he quickly ran through much of his inheritance, and his family placed his money under legal guardianship, leaving him in debt for life. He wrote art criticism, praising Delacroix and later Constantin Guys as the painter of modern life, and translated Poe's tales. Les Fleurs du mal appeared in 1857; he was prosecuted, fined and six poems were banned. A second, expanded edition came out in 1861. Ill with syphilis, he spent two unhappy years in Belgium, suffered a stroke and died in Paris in 1867.

Baudelaire combined classical verse forms with a modern subject matter of city streets, crowds, prostitutes, rag-pickers, boredom and moral decay, and found strange beauty in it. His theory of correspondences, the idea that perfumes, colours and sounds answer each other, inspired the Symbolists. His prose poems helped create a new genre. Verlaine, Rimbaud and Mallarmé followed him, and through them and T. S. Eliot his vision of the modern city entered twentieth-century poetry.

portrait_caption: Gustave Courbet, Portrait of Baudelaire, c. 1848, Musée Fabre

name: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
bio: The great Victorian novelist of Middlemarch, a translator and intellectual who wrote under a male pen name.
bio_full: Mary Ann Evans was born in 1819 on an estate in Warwickshire where her father was a land agent. Intensely religious as a young woman, she lost her faith through reading biblical criticism, and translated David Friedrich Strauss's Life of Jesus (1846) and Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity. In London she became assistant editor of the radical Westminster Review. In 1854 she began living openly with the critic George Henry Lewes, who was married but unable to divorce, a choice that cut her off from respectable society and from her brother. Encouraged by Lewes, she began writing fiction under the name George Eliot, and Adam Bede (1859) was a great success, followed by The Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner, Romola, Middlemarch (1871–72) and Daniel Deronda. After Lewes's death she married John Cross in 1880 and died that December.

George Eliot brought to the novel a philosopher's intelligence and a deep sympathy for ordinary lives. Her narrators reflect on the moral choices and limited horizons of their characters, linking the smallest acts to wider social change, and her psychological analysis prepared the way for Henry James and the modern novel. Virginia Woolf called Middlemarch one of the few English novels written for grown-up people, and it is regularly voted among the greatest novels in English.

portrait_caption: François D'Albert Durade, George Eliot, 1849

name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
bio: The Russian novelist of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov, who dramatised faith, freedom, guilt and suffering with feverish intensity.
bio_full: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821, the son of a doctor at a hospital for the poor; his father was killed in 1839, possibly by his own serfs. He trained as a military engineer but resigned to write, and his first novel, Poor Folk (1846), was hailed by the critic Belinsky. In 1849 he was arrested for membership of the Petrashevsky circle of utopian socialists, sentenced to death and led out to be shot, only to have the sentence commuted at the last moment to four years of hard labour in Siberia followed by army service. He returned to Saint Petersburg in 1859 with epilepsy and a renewed Orthodox faith. Gambling, debts and the deaths of his first wife and brother marked the 1860s, but in Anna Snitkina, his stenographer and second wife, he found stability. Notes from Underground, Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov followed. He died in Saint Petersburg in 1881.

Dostoevsky's novels are dramas of ideas in which characters embody arguments about God, freedom, reason and morality, often in scenes of extreme tension, confession and scandal. The critic Mikhail Bakhtin described them as polyphonic: many voices, none simply the author's. He explored the psychology of guilt, pride and humiliation with an insight that impressed Nietzsche and Freud, and existentialist thinkers from Camus to Sartre saw him as a forerunner. His influence on the twentieth-century novel is immense.

portrait_caption: Vasily Perov, Fyodor Dostoevsky, 1872, Tretyakov Gallery

name: Leo Tolstoy
bio: Count, soldier, novelist and moral prophet, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, often considered the greatest of all novelists.
bio_full: Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy was born in 1828 on his family estate of Yasnaya Polyana, south of Moscow, and was orphaned young. After a dissolute youth and an abandoned university course, he joined the army in the Caucasus and served at the siege of Sevastopol in the Crimean War, which he described in his Sevastopol Sketches. In 1862 he married Sophia Behrs, who bore him thirteen children and copied out his manuscripts. On the estate he wrote War and Peace (1865–69) and Anna Karenina (1875–77). Around 1880 he went through a spiritual crisis, described in A Confession, and developed a radical Christianity rejecting the Church, the state, private property and violence. He was excommunicated in 1901, attracted disciples from around the world and corresponded with Gandhi. In 1910, at eighty-two, he left home secretly and died at the railway station of Astapovo.

Tolstoy's realism is so complete that his novels seem less written than lived: he moves between battlefields and ballrooms, peasants and emperors, with the same clarity and moral attention. He was fascinated by the forces of history, by family life and by death, the subject of The Death of Ivan Ilyich. His later fiction and essays argued for simplicity and non-violent resistance, influencing Gandhi and Martin Luther King. Writers from Flaubert to Virginia Woolf regarded him as the greatest of novelists.

portrait_caption: Ivan Kramskoi, Leo Tolstoy, 1873, Tretyakov Gallery

name: Emily Dickinson
bio: The reclusive Amherst poet who wrote nearly 1,800 compressed, dazzling poems, almost none published in her lifetime.
bio_full: Emily Elizabeth Dickinson was born in 1830 in Amherst, Massachusetts, into a prominent family; her father was a lawyer and congressman. She studied at Amherst Academy and spent a year at Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, but declined to profess the evangelical faith expected of her. From her twenties she withdrew increasingly from society, eventually rarely leaving the family homestead, dressing in white and communicating with friends mainly by letter. Her most productive years were around the Civil War. She sent poems to the critic Thomas Wentworth Higginson, who advised against publication, and only about ten appeared in print during her life, anonymously and altered by editors. She died in Amherst in 1886. Her sister Lavinia then discovered hundreds of poems in a locked box, and the first selection was published in 1890.

Dickinson wrote mostly short poems in the hymn metres of her childhood, made strange by slant rhyme, dashes, capitalised nouns and startling compression. Her subjects are death, faith and doubt, nature, love and the inner life, approached with wit and metaphysical daring. Early editors regularised her punctuation; only Thomas Johnson's 1955 edition and R. W. Franklin's later edition presented the poems as she wrote them. She is now regarded, with Whitman, as one of the two founders of modern American poetry.

name: Lewis Carroll (Charles Lutwidge Dodgson)
bio: Oxford mathematician, logician and photographer who wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass.
bio_full: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson was born in 1832 at Daresbury in Cheshire, the eldest son among eleven children of a clergyman, and entertained his siblings with games, puzzles and magazines. He studied at Christ Church, Oxford, and spent the rest of his life there as a lecturer in mathematics, publishing works on geometry and symbolic logic and becoming an accomplished amateur photographer. On a boat trip in July 1862 he improvised a story for Alice Liddell, the daughter of the dean of Christ Church, and her sisters. Written down and expanded, it was published as Alice's Adventures in Wonderland in 1865 under the pen name Lewis Carroll, with illustrations by John Tenniel. Through the Looking-Glass followed in 1871 and the nonsense poem The Hunting of the Snark in 1876. He died in Guildford in 1898.

Carroll's Alice books turned children's literature away from moral instruction towards play, and their nonsense, puns, parodies of improving verse and logical paradoxes delight adults as much as children. Characters such as the Mad Hatter, the Cheshire Cat and Humpty Dumpty became part of common culture, and his invented words, such as chortle, entered the language. Logicians, philosophers, Surrealists and Joyce have all found something in his work.

name: Henrik Ibsen
bio: The father of modern drama, whose A Doll's House, Ghosts and Hedda Gabler brought social problems and psychological depth to the stage.
bio_full: Henrik Johan Ibsen was born in 1828 in the port town of Skien in Norway; his merchant father went bankrupt when he was a child. At fifteen he was apprenticed to a pharmacist in Grimstad, where he fathered an illegitimate son and wrote his first play. He worked as playwright and director at theatres in Bergen and Christiania for over a decade with little success. In 1864 he left Norway and spent twenty-seven years in Italy and Germany. The verse dramas Brand (1866) and Peer Gynt (1867) made his name in Scandinavia, and he then turned to prose plays about contemporary life: The Pillars of Society, A Doll's House (1879), Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Hedda Gabler (1890) and others. He returned to Norway in 1891 as a national celebrity and died in Christiania in 1906 after a series of strokes.

Ibsen replaced the contrived well-made play with tightly constructed realist drama in which the past gradually emerges to destroy the present, and he dealt openly with marriage, venereal disease, hypocrisy and the individual against society. His heroines, from Nora to Hedda, made him a central figure in debates about women's emancipation, though he said he was writing about human beings. His late plays become increasingly symbolic. Shaw, Strindberg, Chekhov, Joyce and O'Neill all learned from him, and he is among the most performed dramatists in the world.

portrait_caption: Henrik Olrik, Henrik Ibsen, 1879

name: Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens)
bio: Humorist, lecturer and novelist of the Mississippi, author of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.
bio_full: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in 1835 in Florida, Missouri, and grew up in Hannibal on the Mississippi River, the setting of his best-known books. After his father's death he worked as a printer, then as a riverboat pilot until the Civil War closed the river. He went west to Nevada and California, prospected for silver, became a newspaper writer and adopted the pen name Mark Twain, a riverboat call for two fathoms of water. His comic story The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County (1865) and the travel book The Innocents Abroad (1869) made him famous. He married Olivia Langdon and settled in Hartford, Connecticut, where he wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Life on the Mississippi and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884–85). Failed investments bankrupted him in the 1890s, and he paid off his debts with a world lecture tour. The deaths of his wife and two daughters darkened his later writing. He died in 1910.

Twain brought the vernacular speech of ordinary Americans into literature, and his combination of humour, satire and moral seriousness made him the most famous American of his day. His later writings attacked imperialism, racism and religious hypocrisy with growing bitterness. Hemingway claimed that all modern American literature comes from Huckleberry Finn, and Twain remains a symbol of American wit and independence.

name: Émile Zola
bio: Leader of Naturalism and author of the twenty-novel Rougon-Macquart cycle, who risked everything to defend Alfred Dreyfus.
bio_full: Émile Zola was born in Paris in 1840, the son of an Italian engineer, and grew up in Aix-en-Provence, where he was a close friend of Paul Cézanne. His father died when he was seven, leaving the family poor. He failed his baccalaureate, worked in the sales department of the publisher Hachette and as a journalist and art critic, defending Manet and the Impressionists. His novel Thérèse Raquin (1867) brought him notoriety. From 1871 to 1893 he published the Rougon-Macquart, the natural and social history of a family under the Second Empire, whose seventh volume, L'Assommoir (1877), made him rich and famous. In 1898 he published J'accuse, an open letter accusing the army of covering up the wrongful conviction of the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus; convicted of libel, he fled to England for a year. He died in Paris in 1902, asphyxiated by a blocked chimney, and was later reinterred in the Panthéon.

Zola set out to apply the methods of science to the novel, studying heredity and environment and researching each book exhaustively, in the mines, department stores, railways and slums. His Rougon-Macquart novels, including Nana, Germinal and The Beast Within, are powerful, crowded works with an epic, often mythic sweep that goes beyond his theory. His frankness made him a scandal and a bestseller, and his naturalism influenced writers across Europe and America, from Hardy and Gissing to Dreiser.

portrait_caption: Édouard Manet, Émile Zola, 1868, Musée d'Orsay

name: Thomas Hardy
bio: Novelist and poet of the Wessex countryside, author of Tess of the d'Urbervilles and Jude the Obscure, who turned to poetry after the outcry over his last novel.
bio_full: Thomas Hardy was born in 1840 at Higher Bockhampton near Dorchester, the son of a stonemason and builder. He was apprenticed to a local architect and worked in London and Dorset restoring churches, while teaching himself Greek and writing poetry. His first published novel, Desperate Remedies, appeared in 1871, and Far from the Madding Crowd (1874) allowed him to give up architecture. He married Emma Gifford, whom he met while restoring a church in Cornwall. Over the next twenty years he wrote novels set in his fictional Wessex, including The Return of the Native, The Mayor of Casterbridge, Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895). The hostile reception of Jude led him to abandon fiction for poetry, and he published eight collections and the epic drama The Dynasts. After Emma's death in 1912 he wrote moving elegies for her. He died at his Dorchester home, Max Gate, in 1928.

Hardy's novels show people struggling against chance, social convention and an indifferent universe, set against a richly observed rural world that was disappearing. His frank treatment of sexuality and his attacks on marriage and religion shocked Victorian readers. As a poet he wrote in a craggy, varied style about time, memory and loss, and he is now regarded as one of the major English poets of the twentieth century, a strong influence on Larkin and others.

portrait_caption: William Strang, Thomas Hardy, 1893

name: Henry James
bio: The American-born master of the psychological novel, author of The Portrait of a Lady and The Turn of the Screw, who settled in England.
bio_full: Henry James was born in New York in 1843 into a wealthy, intellectual family; his father was a theologian and his brother William became a pioneering psychologist and philosopher. He had a cosmopolitan education in Europe and America and briefly studied law at Harvard. He began publishing stories and reviews in the 1860s and in 1875 moved permanently to Europe, first Paris, where he met Flaubert and Turgenev, and from 1876 London. His novels Daisy Miller, The Portrait of a Lady (1881) and The Bostonians explored Americans abroad and in society. An attempt at a theatrical career ended in humiliation in 1895. He then wrote The Turn of the Screw and, from his house in Rye, the great late novels The Wings of the Dove, The Ambassadors and The Golden Bowl. He became a British subject in 1915, during the First World War, and died in London in 1916.

James was fascinated by the contrast between American innocence and European experience, and by the subtle workings of consciousness, perception and moral choice. He refined the use of a limited point of view and wrote influential prefaces on the art of fiction. His late style, long sentences full of qualifications and deferred meanings, is demanding but rewards close attention. He is a bridge between the nineteenth-century realist novel and Modernism.

portrait_caption: John Singer Sargent, Henry James, 1913, National Portrait Gallery

name: Arthur Rimbaud
bio: The prodigy of French poetry who wrote all his work before twenty-one, including A Season in Hell and Illuminations, then abandoned literature.
bio_full: Jean Nicolas Arthur Rimbaud was born in 1854 at Charleville in the Ardennes and raised by a strict mother after his father, an army officer, left the family. A brilliant pupil, he was writing accomplished Latin and French verse at fifteen. He ran away to Paris several times during the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune. In 1871 he sent poems, including The Drunken Boat, to Paul Verlaine, who invited him to Paris. Their stormy relationship took them to London and Brussels and ended in 1873 when Verlaine shot Rimbaud in the wrist. That year Rimbaud published A Season in Hell. He then gave up poetry, travelled through Europe, enlisted in and deserted from the Dutch colonial army in Java, and worked as a trader in Aden and Harar, Ethiopia, dealing in coffee and guns. A tumour in his leg forced his return to France, where he died in Marseille in 1891 at thirty-seven.

Rimbaud believed that the poet must become a seer through a long, immense and reasoned derangement of all the senses. His poems move from brilliant traditional verse to the prose poems of A Season in Hell and the fragmentary visions of Illuminations, published by Verlaine in 1886. His rebellion, his free verse and his hallucinatory images made him a hero to the Symbolists, the Surrealists, the Beats and rock musicians, and he remains a byword for youthful genius.

portrait_caption: Henri Fantin-Latour, By the Table, 1872, with Verlaine and Rimbaud seated at left, Musée d'Orsay

name: Anton Chekhov
bio: Doctor, short-story writer and dramatist, author of The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard, who reinvented both the short story and the play.
bio_full: Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was born in 1860 in the port of Taganrog on the Sea of Azov, the grandson of a serf. When his father's grocery business failed, the family fled to Moscow, leaving Anton to finish school alone. He studied medicine at Moscow University and supported his family by writing hundreds of comic sketches for magazines. By the late 1880s he was writing serious stories that won him the Pushkin Prize. In 1890 he travelled across Siberia to the penal colony of Sakhalin and wrote a study of it. The failure of The Seagull in 1896 nearly ended his playwriting, but its revival by the Moscow Art Theatre under Stanislavsky in 1898 was a triumph, followed by Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard. Suffering from tuberculosis, he lived mainly in Yalta and in 1901 married the actress Olga Knipper. He died at the German spa of Badenweiler in 1904.

Chekhov's stories and plays avoid melodrama and moral verdicts; they show ordinary people in moments of boredom, longing and missed connection, and leave endings open. In the theatre he made the important happen offstage or beneath the surface of talk, a technique that shaped modern drama. His stories, such as The Lady with the Dog and Ward No. 6, made him a model for short-story writers from Katherine Mansfield to Raymond Carver and Alice Munro.

portrait_caption: Osip Braz, Anton Chekhov, 1898, Tretyakov Gallery

name: Oscar Wilde
bio: Irish wit, playwright and leading voice of Aestheticism, author of The Picture of Dorian Gray and The Importance of Being Earnest, whose career was destroyed by his imprisonment.
bio_full: Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde was born in Dublin in 1854 to a surgeon father and a poet mother who wrote as Speranza. He studied classics at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford, where he came under the influence of Walter Pater and John Ruskin and cultivated the persona of an aesthete. He lectured across America in 1882, married Constance Lloyd and edited a women's magazine. His fairy tales, his only novel The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890–91) and his society comedies, Lady Windermere's Fan, An Ideal Husband and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895), made him the toast of London. In 1895 he sued the Marquess of Queensberry, father of his lover Lord Alfred Douglas, for libel; the case collapsed, and Wilde was convicted of gross indecency and sentenced to two years' hard labour. After prison he wrote De Profundis and The Ballad of Reading Gaol, and died in exile in Paris in 1900.

Wilde championed art for art's sake and turned paradox into an art form, inverting Victorian pieties in epigrams that still circulate. Beneath his comedies of manners lies a sharp critique of hypocrisy, and Dorian Gray is both a Gothic fable and a manifesto of Aestheticism. His persecution made him a symbol of the cost of Victorian sexual morality, and in 2017 he was among the men posthumously pardoned under British law.

portrait_caption: Caricature of Oscar Wilde, Vanity Fair, 1884

name: Joseph Conrad
bio: A Polish-born sea captain who became one of the great novelists in English, author of Heart of Darkness, Lord Jim and Nostromo.
bio_full: Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski was born in 1857 in Berdychiv, in Russian-ruled Ukraine, to Polish noble parents. His father, a poet and patriot, was exiled for conspiring against Russian rule, and both parents died while Conrad was a child. At sixteen he went to Marseille and joined the French merchant navy, then from 1878 the British, rising to the rank of master and becoming a British subject in 1886. In 1890 he captained a river steamer in the Congo Free State, an experience that shocked him and became the basis of Heart of Darkness. He gave up the sea in 1894 and published his first novel, Almayer's Folly, in 1895, writing in English, his third language. Lord Jim, Nostromo, The Secret Agent and Under Western Eyes followed. He lived in Kent with his wife Jessie and died in 1924.

Conrad's fiction deals with isolation, betrayal, honour and the moral darkness of colonialism and political violence. He used complex time schemes and framing narrators, such as Marlow, so that stories are filtered through memory and uncertainty, techniques that link him to Modernism. His view of imperialism has been debated, notably in Chinua Achebe's 1975 critique of Heart of Darkness as racist. His influence reaches Eliot, Faulkner, Fitzgerald, Graham Greene and many later novelists.

name: W. B. Yeats
bio: Irish poet and dramatist, leader of the Irish Literary Revival and winner of the 1923 Nobel Prize, regarded as one of the greatest poets of the twentieth century.
bio_full: William Butler Yeats was born in Dublin in 1865, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats, and grew up between London, Dublin and his mother's home county of Sligo. He studied art, became fascinated by Irish folklore, mysticism and the occult, and in London helped found the Rhymers' Club. In 1889 he met the revolutionary Maud Gonne, whom he loved hopelessly for decades. With Lady Gregory and others he led the Irish Literary Revival and co-founded the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1904. After the Easter Rising of 1916 and Gonne's refusal of him, he married Georgie Hyde-Lees in 1917, whose automatic writing fed his visionary system. He bought a tower, Thoor Ballylee, served as a senator of the new Irish Free State and received the Nobel Prize in 1923. He died in France in 1939.

Yeats's early poetry is lyrical, Romantic and steeped in Celtic myth; from around 1910 he developed a harder, more direct and modern voice, addressing politics, ageing, love and history in poems such as Easter, 1916, The Second Coming, Sailing to Byzantium and Among School Children. His late work is among the most powerful written by any poet in old age. He bridged Victorian Symbolism and Modernism and became the central figure of modern Irish literature.

portrait_caption: John Butler Yeats, William Butler Yeats, 1900

name: Marcel Proust
bio: Author of In Search of Lost Time, a seven-volume novel of memory, time, love and society that is one of the monuments of Modernism.
bio_full: Marcel Proust was born in 1871 in Auteuil, then on the edge of Paris, the son of an eminent doctor and a cultivated mother from a wealthy Jewish family. He suffered from severe asthma from the age of nine. He studied law and philosophy, frequented the aristocratic salons of the Faubourg Saint-Germain and published a book of stories and sketches, Pleasures and Days (1896). He translated John Ruskin and worked for years on an abandoned novel, Jean Santeuil. He was an ardent Dreyfusard. After the deaths of his parents he withdrew increasingly from society, writing at night in a cork-lined bedroom on the Boulevard Haussmann. Swann's Way, the first volume of In Search of Lost Time, was published at his own expense in 1913. Within a Budding Grove won the Prix Goncourt in 1919. He died of pneumonia in 1922, still revising; the last three volumes appeared after his death.

Proust's novel follows its narrator from childhood through the high society of the Belle Époque and the First World War to his discovery that involuntary memory, triggered by sensations such as the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea, can recover the past, and that art can preserve it. His long, intricate sentences trace the movement of thought and feeling, and his analyses of jealousy, snobbery, desire and homosexuality were revolutionary. He influenced novelists and thinkers across the century and remains a touchstone for writing about memory.

portrait_caption: Jacques-Émile Blanche, Marcel Proust, 1892, Musée d'Orsay

name: Thomas Mann
bio: The German novelist of Buddenbrooks, Death in Venice and The Magic Mountain, winner of the 1929 Nobel Prize and an exiled opponent of Nazism.
bio_full: Paul Thomas Mann was born in 1875 into a patrician merchant family in Lübeck. After his father's death and the liquidation of the family firm, he moved to Munich, worked briefly in insurance and on a satirical magazine, and published Buddenbrooks (1901), a novel of a merchant family's decline based on his own, which made him famous. Death in Venice followed in 1912. He married Katia Pringsheim, and their children included the writers Klaus and Erika Mann. During the First World War he defended German nationalism, but in the 1920s he became a supporter of the Weimar Republic. The Magic Mountain appeared in 1924, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1929. In 1933 he went into exile, first in Switzerland, then from 1938 in the United States, where he broadcast speeches against Hitler and wrote Joseph and His Brothers and Doctor Faustus. He returned to Switzerland in 1952 and died near Zurich in 1955.

Mann's novels are large, ironic and full of ideas, exploring the conflict between art and life, the bourgeois and the artist, health and disease, and the fate of German culture. He used leitmotifs, recurring phrases associated with characters in the manner of Wagner, and blended realism with myth and philosophical debate. He is regarded as the leading German novelist of the twentieth century.

name: Rainer Maria Rilke
bio: The Prague-born poet of the Duino Elegies and the Sonnets to Orpheus, one of the most intense and spiritual lyric voices in German.
bio_full: René Maria Rilke was born in Prague in 1875 to a German-speaking family; his unhappy schooling at military academies left lasting scars. He studied in Prague and Munich, where he met Lou Andreas-Salomé, who became his lover and lifelong confidante and with whom he travelled twice to Russia. He married the sculptor Clara Westhoff in 1901 but lived mostly apart from her. In Paris he worked for a time as secretary to Rodin, whose dedication to looking taught him to write his New Poems, and he wrote his only novel, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge. In 1912, at the castle of Duino near Trieste, he began the Duino Elegies, but the war interrupted him for a decade. Settling in the Swiss château of Muzot, he completed the Elegies and wrote the Sonnets to Orpheus in a burst in February 1922. He died of leukaemia in 1926.

Rilke's poetry moves from the precise, sculptural thing-poems of the Paris years to the vast meditations of the Elegies on angels, death, love and the human task of transforming the visible world into inner experience. His Letters to a Young Poet are widely read for their advice on solitude and art. He has been translated into English more often than almost any other modern poet.

name: James Joyce
bio: The Irish exile who wrote Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Ulysses and Finnegans Wake, transforming the possibilities of the novel.
bio_full: James Augustine Aloysius Joyce was born in 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest surviving child of a large family that slid into poverty through his father's improvidence. Educated by the Jesuits and at University College Dublin, he rejected Catholicism and Irish nationalism, and in 1904 left Ireland with Nora Barnacle, whom he married only in 1931. They lived in Trieste, Zurich and from 1920 Paris, where Joyce taught English and struggled with poverty and worsening eye disease. Dubliners appeared in 1914 after years of disputes with publishers, and A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was serialised in 1914–15. Ulysses, partly serialised in an American magazine whose editors were prosecuted for obscenity, was published in Paris by Sylvia Beach in 1922. He spent seventeen years on Finnegans Wake (1939). Fleeing the German occupation of France, he returned to Zurich, where he died in 1941.

Joyce made Dublin the setting of all his fiction and from it created universal works. In Ulysses he combined an epic structure taken from the Odyssey with stream of consciousness, each chapter in a different style, and a frankness that led to bans in Britain and the United States. Finnegans Wake pushes language into multilingual puns and dream logic. He is widely regarded as the most influential novelist of the twentieth century, and Bloomsday, 16 June, the day on which Ulysses is set, is celebrated around the world.

portrait_caption: Jacques-Émile Blanche, James Joyce, 1934

name: Franz Kafka
bio: The Prague insurance lawyer whose stories and novels, The Metamorphosis, The Trial and The Castle, gave the world the word Kafkaesque.
bio_full: Franz Kafka was born in Prague in 1883 into a German-speaking Jewish family; his domineering father, a self-made shopkeeper, overshadowed his life, as he described in his unsent Letter to His Father. He studied law and from 1908 worked at the Workers' Accident Insurance Institute, writing in the evenings and at night. He published only a few stories in his lifetime, including The Judgement, The Metamorphosis (1915), In the Penal Colony and A Hunger Artist. He was engaged twice to Felice Bauer and once to Julie Wohryzek, and had an intense correspondence with Milena Jesenská. Diagnosed with tuberculosis in 1917, he retired in 1922 and spent his last months in Berlin with Dora Diamant. He died at a sanatorium near Vienna in 1924. He asked his friend Max Brod to burn his manuscripts; Brod refused, and published The Trial, The Castle and Amerika.

Kafka's fiction describes nightmarish situations in calm, precise prose: a man wakes as a giant insect, another is arrested and tried for an unnamed crime, a land surveyor can never reach the castle. His works have been read as religious allegories, as critiques of bureaucracy and power, as expressions of Jewish experience or of the individual's alienation in the modern world, and they resist any single interpretation. His influence on twentieth-century literature, from Borges and Camus to García Márquez, is immense.

name: Virginia Woolf
bio: Novelist and essayist of the Bloomsbury Group, author of Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and A Room of One's Own.
bio_full: Adeline Virginia Stephen was born in London in 1882, the daughter of the critic and editor Sir Leslie Stephen. Educated at home in her father's library, she suffered the deaths of her mother, half-sister and father in close succession, and the first of several severe breakdowns. With her siblings she moved to Bloomsbury, where their friends formed the Bloomsbury Group of writers, artists and thinkers. In 1912 she married the writer Leonard Woolf, and in 1917 they founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work as well as T. S. Eliot and the first English translations of Freud. Her novels include Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), Orlando, inspired by her love for Vita Sackville-West, and The Waves. Her essays include A Room of One's Own (1929) and Three Guineas. During the Second World War, fearing another breakdown, she drowned herself in the River Ouse in 1941.

Woolf wanted to record the atoms as they fall upon the mind, and her novels follow the flow of consciousness of several characters, moving freely between present perception and memory, often within a single day. Her lyrical style and experiments with time and point of view made her a central figure of Modernism. Her essays on women and writing, especially the argument that a woman must have money and a room of her own to write fiction, made her a founding figure of feminist criticism.

portrait_caption: Roger Fry, Virginia Woolf, c. 1917

name: T. S. Eliot
bio: Poet, critic and dramatist whose The Waste Land defined Modernist poetry. He won the Nobel Prize in 1948.
bio_full: Thomas Stearns Eliot was born in 1888 in St Louis, Missouri, into a distinguished New England family. He studied philosophy at Harvard, the Sorbonne and Oxford and in 1914 met Ezra Pound in London, who arranged the publication of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock in 1915. That year he married Vivienne Haigh-Wood; the marriage was deeply unhappy. He worked as a teacher and for eight years in the foreign department of Lloyds Bank, while writing criticism and editing the journal The Criterion. The Waste Land (1922), edited by Pound, made him the most influential poet of his generation. In 1925 he joined the publisher Faber and Gwyer, later Faber and Faber, where he remained for life. In 1927 he became a British subject and was received into the Church of England. He wrote Four Quartets and verse plays such as Murder in the Cathedral, received the Nobel Prize in 1948 and died in London in 1965.

Eliot's early poems use fragmentation, allusion, multiple voices and the sordid imagery of the modern city to express spiritual emptiness, while his later work, culminating in Four Quartets, is meditative and religious. His essays, such as Tradition and the Individual Talent, shaped literary criticism for decades. Admired as the leading poet of Modernism, he has also been criticised for antisemitic passages in some early poems. His light verse Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats became the musical Cats.

name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
bio: The chronicler of the Jazz Age, author of The Great Gatsby and Tender Is the Night.
bio_full: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was born in 1896 in St Paul, Minnesota, and studied at Princeton, which he left to join the army in 1917, though he was never sent overseas. While stationed in Alabama he met Zelda Sayre, who agreed to marry him after his first novel, This Side of Paradise (1920), became a bestseller. The couple became celebrities of the Jazz Age, living extravagantly in New York, on the French Riviera and in Paris, where Fitzgerald befriended Hemingway. The Great Gatsby (1925) was admired by critics but sold modestly. Zelda's mental illness, beginning in 1930, and his own alcoholism and debts darkened the following years; Tender Is the Night (1934) was a commercial failure. He worked as a Hollywood screenwriter and died of a heart attack in 1940, aged forty-four, leaving The Last Tycoon unfinished.

Fitzgerald wrote with lyrical precision about wealth, glamour, ambition and disillusion, and about the American Dream and its corruption. He supported himself mostly with stories for popular magazines, such as Babylon Revisited and The Diamond as Big as the Ritz. He died believing himself a failure, but the revival of interest after the Second World War made The Great Gatsby one of the most widely read American novels.

name: William Faulkner
bio: The novelist of the American South, whose fictional Yoknapatawpha County holds The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom!
bio_full: William Cuthbert Falkner, who later added the u, was born in 1897 in New Albany, Mississippi, and grew up in Oxford, Mississippi, the town where he spent most of his life. He trained with the Royal Air Force in Canada in 1918 but the war ended before he saw action. He attended the University of Mississippi briefly, worked odd jobs, including as postmaster, and was encouraged by Sherwood Anderson to write about his native region. In 1929 he published Sartoris and The Sound and the Fury, beginning his saga of Yoknapatawpha County, followed by As I Lay Dying, Light in August, Absalom, Absalom! and Go Down, Moses. To earn money he wrote screenplays in Hollywood, including for The Big Sleep. His reputation, low in the late 1930s, revived in the 1940s, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1949. He died in 1962.

Faulkner used stream of consciousness, multiple narrators, fractured chronology and long, rhetorical sentences to explore the burden of history, race, family and memory in the South after slavery and the Civil War. His idea that the past is never dead runs through all his work. He influenced writers across the Americas, notably García Márquez and the Latin American Boom.

name: Ernest Hemingway
bio: The writer whose terse, understated prose transformed twentieth-century fiction, author of The Sun Also Rises and The Old Man and the Sea.
bio_full: Ernest Miller Hemingway was born in 1899 in Oak Park, Illinois, and worked as a reporter for the Kansas City Star before volunteering as an ambulance driver in Italy in the First World War, where he was badly wounded in 1918. In the 1920s he lived in Paris as a foreign correspondent, mixing with Gertrude Stein, Ezra Pound, Fitzgerald and Joyce, and published the stories of In Our Time and the novel The Sun Also Rises (1926), followed by A Farewell to Arms (1929). He later lived in Key West and Cuba, reported on the Spanish Civil War, which inspired For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), and covered the Second World War in Europe. Married four times, he cultivated a public image of big-game hunter, fisherman and war correspondent. The Old Man and the Sea (1952) won the Pulitzer Prize, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1954. Suffering from depression and ill health, he died by suicide in Ketchum, Idaho, in 1961.

Hemingway's style, short declarative sentences, plain words, repetition and dialogue, aimed to convey emotion by leaving it unsaid, an approach he compared to an iceberg with most of its mass beneath the surface. His themes are war, love, loss, courage and stoic endurance. His influence on prose in English, from hard-boiled crime fiction to minimalism, has been enormous, while his portrayal of masculinity and of women has been much debated.

name: Jorge Luis Borges
bio: The Argentine master of the short story and essay, whose labyrinths, libraries and mirrors anticipated postmodern fiction.
bio_full: Jorge Luis Borges was born in Buenos Aires in 1899 into a bilingual family and learned English before Spanish. His family lived in Geneva during the First World War and then in Spain, where he joined the avant-garde Ultraist movement. Returning to Buenos Aires in 1921, he published poetry and essays and co-founded literary magazines. A serious head injury in 1938 was followed by the stories of his greatest period, collected in Ficciones (1944) and The Aleph (1949). Under Perón he was removed from his post at a municipal library. After Perón's fall he became director of the National Library in 1955, by which time he was almost blind, and taught English literature at the University of Buenos Aires. International fame came after he shared the Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett in 1961. He died in Geneva in 1986.

Borges's short stories are compressed philosophical fictions about infinity, time, identity and the nature of books, often disguised as essays, reviews or encyclopaedia entries. Their erudition, irony and play with invented sources made him a precursor of postmodernism and a key influence on writers such as Calvino, Eco and García Márquez. He wrote poetry throughout his life and is regarded as one of the most important writers in Spanish of the twentieth century.

name: Pablo Neruda
bio: Chilean poet of love and politics, author of Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair and Canto General, and winner of the 1971 Nobel Prize.
bio_full: Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto was born in 1904 in Parral, Chile, and grew up in Temuco in the south; he adopted the pen name Pablo Neruda as a teenager. His second book, Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair (1924), made him famous at twenty. He served as a consul in Burma, Ceylon, Java, Spain and Mexico, and the Spanish Civil War and the murder of his friend Lorca turned him to political poetry. He joined the Chilean Communist Party and was elected senator in 1945, but went into hiding and exile in 1948 after the party was banned. His epic Canto General (1950) traces the history of the Americas. He returned to Chile in 1952, received the Nobel Prize in 1971 and served as ambassador to France under Salvador Allende. He died in Santiago in September 1973, days after the military coup; the cause of his death has been disputed.

Neruda's poetry ranges from sensual love lyrics and the dark, surreal Residence on Earth to political epic and the simple, celebratory Elemental Odes to everyday things. Gabriel García Márquez called him the greatest poet of the twentieth century in any language. He remains one of the most widely read poets in the world.

name: George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair)
bio: The essayist and novelist of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, whose name became a byword for warnings against totalitarianism.
bio_full: Eric Arthur Blair was born in 1903 in Motihari, India, where his father worked for the opium department, and was educated in England at Eton. He served in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma from 1922 to 1927, an experience that turned him against imperialism. He then deliberately lived among the poor in Paris and London, writing Down and Out in Paris and London (1933) under the name George Orwell, and investigated working-class life in The Road to Wigan Pier. In 1936 he fought with the POUM militia in the Spanish Civil War, was shot in the throat and fled the communist purge of his comrades, as he recorded in Homage to Catalonia. During the Second World War he worked for the BBC and as literary editor of the Tribune. Animal Farm (1945) brought him fame. Already ill with tuberculosis, he wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four on the Scottish island of Jura and died in London in 1950.

Orwell was a democratic socialist who opposed both fascism and Soviet communism. His plain, vigorous prose and essays such as Politics and the English Language and Shooting an Elephant made him one of the great English essayists. Words he coined or popularised, such as Big Brother, doublethink and thoughtcrime, entered everyday language, and the adjective Orwellian describes the abuse of language and surveillance by the state.

name: Vladimir Nabokov
bio: The Russian-born novelist who wrote in two languages, author of Lolita and Pale Fire, and a dazzling stylist and lepidopterist.
bio_full: Vladimir Vladimirovich Nabokov was born in Saint Petersburg in 1899 into a wealthy aristocratic family; his father was a liberal politician. After the Revolution the family fled to Western Europe, and Nabokov studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. In Berlin in 1922 his father was killed shielding another man from an assassin. Under the pen name V. Sirin, Nabokov became the leading writer of the Russian émigré community, with novels such as The Defence and The Gift. In 1940 he fled with his Jewish wife Véra and their son to the United States, where he taught at Wellesley and Cornell, worked on butterflies at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology and began writing in English. Lolita, rejected by American publishers, appeared in Paris in 1955 and became an international scandal and bestseller. He moved to Montreux, Switzerland, in 1961, where he wrote Pale Fire and Ada, and died in 1977.

Nabokov's fiction is full of wordplay, puzzles, unreliable narrators and parodies, written in a richly allusive, sensuous prose in his adopted English. He insisted on the primacy of style and detail and scorned novels of ideas. Lolita, narrated by a paedophile, remains controversial for its subject and admired for its artistry, while Pale Fire, a poem with a mad commentary, is a landmark of postmodern form.

name: Albert Camus
bio: The French-Algerian novelist and essayist of The Stranger, The Plague and The Myth of Sisyphus, winner of the 1957 Nobel Prize.
bio_full: Albert Camus was born in 1913 in Mondovi in French Algeria. His father was killed in the First World War, and he grew up in poverty in Algiers with his nearly deaf, illiterate mother. A scholarship took him to the lycée and the University of Algiers, where he studied philosophy, played football and contracted tuberculosis. He worked as a journalist and ran a theatre company. In 1942, in occupied France, he published The Stranger and the essay The Myth of Sisyphus, and he became editor of the Resistance newspaper Combat. The Plague (1947) and the essay The Rebel (1951), which led to a break with Sartre, followed. He was troubled by the Algerian War, condemning both terrorism and colonial repression. He received the Nobel Prize in 1957, aged forty-four, and died in a car accident in 1960.

Camus explored the absurd, the conflict between the human need for meaning and the silent universe, and argued for lucid revolt, solidarity and moderation rather than despair or ideology. He rejected the label existentialist, though he is often grouped with Sartre. His clear, classical style and moral seriousness made him one of the most widely read French writers of the twentieth century.

name: Samuel Beckett
bio: Irish playwright and novelist, writing in English and French, whose Waiting for Godot is the landmark of the Theatre of the Absurd. Nobel Prize 1969.
bio_full: Samuel Barclay Beckett was born in 1906 in Foxrock, near Dublin, into a Protestant middle-class family. He studied French and Italian at Trinity College Dublin and in 1928 went to Paris as a lecturer, where he became a friend and assistant of James Joyce. He published essays, stories and the novel Murphy (1938), and settled in Paris permanently. During the Second World War he joined the French Resistance and later hid in the south of France. After the war, writing mainly in French, he produced his most important work: the novels Molloy, Malone Dies and The Unnamable, and the play Waiting for Godot, which premiered in Paris in 1953 and became an international sensation. Endgame, Krapp's Last Tape and Happy Days followed. He received the Nobel Prize in 1969 and died in Paris in 1989.

Beckett pared drama and fiction down to their bare essentials: characters waiting, talking, failing and going on in empty spaces, with bleak humour drawn from music hall and silent film. His work deals with time, memory, habit and the difficulty of meaning, and became increasingly minimal in late plays such as Not I. He translated most of his own works between French and English, and he is regarded as one of the most important dramatists of the twentieth century.

name: Gabriel García Márquez
bio: Colombian novelist and journalist, master of magical realism and author of One Hundred Years of Solitude. Nobel Prize 1982.
bio_full: Gabriel José García Márquez was born in 1927 in Aracataca, a town in Colombia's Caribbean region, and was raised in his early years by his maternal grandparents, whose stories of war and superstition shaped his imagination. He studied law in Bogotá but left to become a journalist, working in Cartagena, Barranquilla and Bogotá and as a correspondent in Europe. His early fiction, including No One Writes to the Colonel, was little noticed. Living in Mexico City, he wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude in about eighteen months; published in Buenos Aires in 1967, it became a phenomenon across the Spanish-speaking world and then internationally. The Autumn of the Patriarch, Chronicle of a Death Foretold and Love in the Time of Cholera followed. He received the Nobel Prize in 1982, remained a political journalist and friend of Fidel Castro, and died in Mexico City in 2014.

García Márquez combined the matter-of-fact narration of his grandmother's tales with the techniques of Faulkner and Kafka, presenting marvels and miracles as ordinary events, a style that became known as magical realism. His fiction explores solitude, power, memory and the cycles of Latin American history. He is the best-known writer of the Latin American Boom and one of the most widely read novelists of the twentieth century.

name: Italo Calvino
bio: Italian writer of fables, fantasies and formal experiments, including Invisible Cities and If on a winter's night a traveller.
bio_full: Italo Calvino was born in 1923 near Havana, Cuba, where his Italian parents were working as agronomists, and grew up in Sanremo on the Italian Riviera. During the Second World War he joined the communist partisans in the Ligurian mountains, the background of his first novel, The Path to the Spiders' Nests (1947). He worked for decades as an editor at the Einaudi publishing house in Turin and left the Communist Party after the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956. His trilogy Our Ancestors, including The Baron in the Trees, and his collection of Italian Folktales established him. Living in Paris from 1967, he joined the Oulipo group of experimental writers. Invisible Cities (1972) and If on a winter's night a traveller (1979) followed. He died in Siena in 1985 while preparing the lectures later published as Six Memos for the Next Millennium.

Calvino moved from neorealism to fantasy and to fiction built on combinatory rules and games, but his work is always light, clear and playful, informed by science, folk tale and a deep curiosity about how stories are made. He is one of the key figures of postmodern fiction and among the most translated Italian writers of the century.

name: Toni Morrison
bio: American novelist of Beloved and Song of Solomon, who placed African American history and experience at the centre of the novel. Nobel Prize 1993.
bio_full: Chloe Ardelia Wofford was born in 1931 in Lorain, Ohio, into a working-class family whose stories and songs she later drew on. She took the name Toni at Howard University, where she studied English, and earned a master's degree at Cornell. She taught at Howard, married and divorced, and in 1965 became an editor at Random House, where she published and championed African American writers. Her first novel, The Bluest Eye, appeared in 1970, followed by Sula, Song of Solomon (1977) and Tar Baby. Beloved (1987) won the Pulitzer Prize. In 1993 she became the first African American woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. She taught at Princeton for many years and continued to publish novels, essays and criticism, including Playing in the Dark. She died in 2019.

Morrison wrote lyrical, layered novels that combine shifting points of view, myth, folklore and the supernatural with an unflinching treatment of slavery, racism, community and love. She wrote, as she said, without explaining Black life to a white gaze. Her work transformed the American canon and is widely taught around the world.
